rash.name: Rash
rash.what: Any change in the colour or texture of the skin. Most rashes are harmless reactions, infections or inflammatory skin conditions; a few signal serious illness, especially when they come with fever, spread quickly or do not fade under pressure.

commonCauses.name: Eczema (atopic dermatitis)
commonCauses.note: Dry, itchy patches in the creases of elbows and knees.

commonCauses.name: Contact dermatitis and irritants
commonCauses.note: Red itchy skin where something touched it: nickel, detergents, plants.

commonCauses.name: Hives (urticaria)
commonCauses.note: Itchy raised wheals that move around within hours, from allergy, infection or no clear cause.

commonCauses.name: Viral rashes
commonCauses.note: Chickenpox, measles, slapped cheek, hand-foot-and-mouth; often with fever.

commonCauses.name: Fungal infections
commonCauses.note: Ringworm, athlete's foot, thrush.

commonCauses.name: Psoriasis
commonCauses.note: Well-defined red plaques with silvery scale on elbows, knees and scalp.

lessCommon.name: Meningococcal sepsis
lessCommon.note: Purple spots or bruises that do not fade under a glass, with fever and being very unwell.

lessCommon.name: Drug reactions
lessCommon.note: Widespread rash days after starting a medicine; blistering or peeling is an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Shingles
lessCommon.note: A painful band of blisters on one side of the body.

lessCommon.name: Cellulitis
lessCommon.note: Spreading, hot, tender redness.

lessCommon.name: Autoimmune disease
lessCommon.note: Butterfly rash of lupus, the rash of dermatomyositis.

lessCommon.name: Skin cancer
lessCommon.note: A changing mole or a sore that will not heal.

urgent: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, especially with fever or drowsiness
A rash with swelling of the face or tongue, wheeze or difficulty breathing
Blistering, peeling skin, or a rash affecting the mouth, eyes or genitals after a new medicine
A rapidly spreading hot, painful rash with fever

numbness.name: Numbness
numbness.what: Reduced or absent feeling in part of the body. Its distribution maps the fault: a glove or stocking pattern points to a general nerve disorder (neuropathy), a single nerve's territory to compression, one side of the body to the brain or spinal cord.

commonCauses.name: Pressure on a nerve
commonCauses.note: Sitting on a foot, sleeping on an arm: resolves in minutes.

commonCauses.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
commonCauses.note: Numb thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night, from median nerve compression at the wrist.

commonCauses.name: Sciatica or a trapped nerve in the neck
commonCauses.note: Numbness in a strip down the leg or arm with back or neck pain.

commonCauses.name: Peripheral neuropathy
commonCauses.note: Gradual glove-and-stocking numbness from diabetes, alcohol, vitamin B12 deficiency or chemotherapy.

commonCauses.name: Migraine aura
commonCauses.note: Tingling spreading up an arm to the face over minutes, followed by headache.

commonCauses.name: Hyperventilation and anxiety
commonCauses.note: Numbness around the mouth and fingertips.

lessCommon.name: Stroke or transient ischaemic attack
lessCommon.note: Sudden numbness of the face, arm or leg on one side.

lessCommon.name: Multiple sclerosis
lessCommon.note: Episodes of numbness lasting days to weeks, often with vision or balance problems.

lessCommon.name: Spinal cord compression
lessCommon.note: Numbness below a level on the trunk with weakness and bladder problems.

lessCommon.name: Cauda equina syndrome
lessCommon.note: Numbness in the saddle area with bladder or bowel disturbance.

lessCommon.name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
lessCommon.note: Ascending numbness and weakness over days after an infection.

urgent: Sudden numbness on one side of the body, face droop or slurred speech: possible stroke, call emergency services
Numbness in the saddle area with difficulty passing urine or controlling bowels
Rapidly spreading numbness and weakness
Numbness after a neck or back injury

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

tingling.name: Tingling (pins and needles)
tingling.what: Prickling, buzzing or crawling sensations without an outside cause, produced when sensory nerves fire abnormally. Brief tingling from pressure is universal; persistent or spreading tingling has the same causes as numbness and is investigated the same way.

commonCauses.name: Pressure on a nerve or reduced blood flow
commonCauses.note: Crossed legs, tight straps, cold hands.

commonCauses.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar nerve entrapment
commonCauses.note: Tingling in specific fingers, worse at night or leaning on the elbow.

commonCauses.name: Cervical or lumbar nerve root irritation
commonCauses.note: Tingling down an arm or leg with neck or back pain.

commonCauses.name: Hyperventilation
commonCauses.note: Tingling around the lips and in both hands during panic or over-breathing.

commonCauses.name: Peripheral neuropathy
commonCauses.note: Diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, some medicines.

lessCommon.name: Stroke or TIA
lessCommon.note: Sudden one-sided tingling with weakness or speech difficulty.

lessCommon.name: Multiple sclerosis
lessCommon.note: Tingling that spreads over days, sometimes an electric shock down the spine on bending the neck.

lessCommon.name: Low calcium or other electrolyte disturbance
lessCommon.note: Tingling around the mouth and cramps.

lessCommon.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
lessCommon.note: Tingling feet with unsteadiness and anaemia.

lessCommon.name: Raynaud's phenomenon
lessCommon.note: Fingers turn white then blue and tingle in the cold.

urgent: Sudden tingling on one side with weakness, face droop or difficulty speaking
Tingling spreading rapidly up the legs or arms over hours to days
Tingling with severe headache, neck injury or loss of bladder control

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

weakness.name: Weakness
weakness.what: Loss of muscle power, distinct from tiredness or heaviness. True weakness means a muscle cannot do what it could before, and its pattern (one side, one limb, both legs, face and eyes, or everywhere) points to the brain, spinal cord, nerve, junction or muscle.

commonCauses.name: Deconditioning, illness and age
commonCauses.note: Generalised weakness after bed rest, infection or with muscle loss in older age.

commonCauses.name: Nerve compression
commonCauses.note: Foot drop from a slipped disc, wrist weakness from radial nerve pressure, hand weakness from carpal tunnel or ulnar nerve entrapment.

commonCauses.name: Bell's palsy
commonCauses.note: Sudden weakness of one side of the face including the forehead.

commonCauses.name: Low potassium, thyroid disease, steroids
commonCauses.note: Generalised or proximal weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, lifting arms).

commonCauses.name: Statin and other drug-induced myopathy
commonCauses.note: Aching weak thighs and shoulders.

lessCommon.name: Stroke and TIA
lessCommon.note: Sudden weakness of the face, arm or leg on one side.

lessCommon.name: Spinal cord compression
lessCommon.note: Weakness of both legs with numbness and bladder problems.

lessCommon.name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
lessCommon.note: Ascending weakness over days, can affect breathing.

lessCommon.name: Myasthenia gravis
lessCommon.note: Fatigable weakness: drooping eyelids, double vision, worse as the day goes on.

lessCommon.name: Motor neurone disease and muscular dystrophies
lessCommon.note: Progressive weakness with wasting or twitching.

lessCommon.name: Multiple sclerosis
lessCommon.note: Episodes of weakness, numbness or vision loss.

urgent: Sudden weakness of the face, arm or leg, especially on one side: call emergency services (stroke)
Weakness of both legs, or weakness with loss of bladder or bowel control
Weakness that spreads over hours or days, or affects swallowing or breathing
Weakness after a head, neck or back injury

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

joint-pain.name: Joint pain
joint-pain.what: Pain in one or more joints. One hot swollen joint, several symmetrical swollen joints, and aching joints without swelling are three different problems: infection or crystals, inflammatory arthritis, and wear or viral illness respectively.

commonCauses.name: Osteoarthritis
commonCauses.note: Wear of cartilage in knees, hips, hands and spine; pain with use, stiffness after rest.

commonCauses.name: Injury and overuse
commonCauses.note: Sprains, tendon and bursa inflammation.

commonCauses.name: Viral infections
commonCauses.note: Aching joints with flu, parvovirus, rubella, chikungunya and others.

commonCauses.name: Gout
commonCauses.note: Sudden agonising red joint, classically the big toe.

commonCauses.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
commonCauses.note: Symmetrical swelling of small joints of hands and feet with morning stiffness over an hour.

lessCommon.name: Septic arthritis
lessCommon.note: A single hot swollen joint with fever; an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis
lessCommon.note: Inflammatory arthritis linked to psoriasis, the spine or a recent infection.

lessCommon.name: Lupus and other connective tissue diseases
lessCommon.note: Joint pain with rash, mouth ulcers, fatigue.

lessCommon.name: Lyme disease
lessCommon.note: Swollen knee weeks after a tick bite.

lessCommon.name: Haemophilia and leukaemia
lessCommon.note: Joint bleeding or bone pain in children.

urgent: A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever or inability to move it
Joint pain with a rash that does not fade under pressure
Joint pain after injury with deformity or inability to bear weight

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

breast-lump.name: Breast lump
breast-lump.what: A new lump, or an area of thickening that feels different from the rest of the breast, anywhere in the breast tissue, which extends from about the second to the sixth rib and up into the armpit as the axillary tail. Breast tissue is a mixture of glands, ducts and fat that changes with the menstrual cycle, pregnancy, breastfeeding and age, so lumpiness that comes and goes with periods is common. Most lumps are benign, but no lump can be reliably sorted by touch alone: a new lump is assessed at a breast clinic by triple assessment, meaning clinical examination, imaging (mammography, usually with ultrasound, or ultrasound alone in younger people) and, where needed, a needle biopsy. Breast screening is offered to people who have no symptoms; a new lump should not wait for the next screening appointment, and a normal recent screening mammogram does not exclude cancer in a lump found since. Men have a small amount of breast tissue behind the nipple, trans women on oestrogen develop breast tissue, and trans men who have had chest surgery retain some, so a lump needs the same assessment in everyone.

commonCauses.name: Fibroadenoma
commonCauses.note: A smooth, firm, rubbery lump that moves easily under the fingers, most common in teenagers and women in their twenties and thirties; benign, and often simply monitored once confirmed.

commonCauses.name: Breast cyst
commonCauses.note: A fluid-filled sac that can appear quickly, feel smooth and tense or tender, and vary with the cycle; most common from the forties up to the menopause. Ultrasound confirms it and draining it with a needle relieves it.

commonCauses.name: Fibrocystic change
commonCauses.note: Generalised lumpiness or ropiness, often in the upper outer part of the breast, tender in the days before a period and settling afterwards; a normal variation rather than a disease.

commonCauses.name: Mastitis and breast abscess
commonCauses.note: Infection, most often during breastfeeding, causing a hot, red, painful, swollen area with fever; an abscess forms a tender, fluctuant lump that needs draining.

commonCauses.name: Fat necrosis and lipoma
commonCauses.note: A firm lump after a knock, injury or surgery to the breast (fat necrosis) can mimic cancer and needs imaging to confirm; a lipoma is a soft, benign lump of fatty tissue.

lessCommon.name: Breast cancer
lessCommon.note: Typically a hard, irregular, painless lump that feels fixed to the surrounding tissue, sometimes with skin dimpling, a newly inverted nipple, nipple discharge or a lump in the armpit. Risk rises steeply with age; it is rare in men but does occur.

lessCommon.name: Phyllodes tumour
lessCommon.note: An uncommon, often fast-growing lump that resembles a fibroadenoma; most are benign, but they can recur or occasionally be malignant, so they are removed.

lessCommon.name: Gynaecomastia in men
lessCommon.note: Enlargement of the glandular tissue behind the nipple, usually on both sides and sometimes tender, common at puberty and in older age; it may follow hormone changes, liver disease or medicines. A firm one-sided lump away from the nipple is assessed for cancer.

lessCommon.name: Lumps after gender-affirming care
lessCommon.note: Trans women on oestrogen develop breast tissue and can form the same benign and malignant lumps as cisgender women; trans men who have had chest masculinisation surgery keep a thin layer of breast tissue, so a lump on the chest wall still needs assessment. Breast screening invitations depend on how a person is registered with their GP: trans women who have been on gender-affirming hormones for several years and trans men who have not had chest surgery are eligible, and may need to ask to be invited. A new lump is assessed in the same way in everyone and should not wait for screening.

urgent: Any new lump or area of thickening in the breast or armpit, in anyone, which needs a GP appointment within days rather than weeks
Dimpling, puckering or redness of the skin, or a change in the size or shape of one breast
A nipple that has newly turned inwards, a rash or crusting around the nipple, or blood-stained discharge
A hot, red, swollen, painful breast with fever, which may be an abscess needing drainage
A lump that has been checked before but has since grown or changed

heavy-periods.name: Heavy periods
heavy-periods.what: Menstrual bleeding that is heavier or lasts longer than usual and gets in the way of daily life. A measured loss of more than about 80 mL a cycle is the textbook threshold, but blood loss is rarely measured; in practice heavy periods mean needing to change a pad or tampon every one to two hours, using two forms of protection at once, passing clots larger than about 2.5 cm, bleeding through clothes or bedding, or bleeding for more than seven days. The blood comes from the endometrium, the lining of the uterus that is shed each cycle, and loss is increased by anything that enlarges the cavity, thickens the lining or weakens clotting. The pattern matters: regular but heavy periods, irregular heavy bleeds after long gaps, and heavy periods with bleeding in between point to different causes. Persistent heavy loss is a leading cause of iron deficiency anaemia. The same assessment applies to trans men and non-binary people who have periods. Heavy periods are worth raising with a GP whenever they interfere with daily life, school or work, because they can be assessed and treated; they do not have to be put up with.

commonCauses.name: No underlying cause found
commonCauses.note: In a large proportion of cases examination and tests are normal; the periods are regular but heavy, and treatment is directed at the bleeding itself.

commonCauses.name: Fibroids and polyps
commonCauses.note: Benign growths of the uterine muscle (fibroids) or of the lining (endometrial polyps) enlarge the bleeding surface; fibroids that bulge into the cavity cause the heaviest bleeding.

commonCauses.name: Adenomyosis and endometriosis
commonCauses.note: Endometrial-like tissue within the muscle wall of the uterus (adenomyosis) typically causes heavy, painful periods with a bulky, tender uterus; endometriosis, where similar tissue grows outside the uterus, more often causes painful periods, pain during or after sex and pelvic pain, and can occur alongside it.

commonCauses.name: Irregular ovulation
commonCauses.note: When ovulation is infrequent, as in polycystic ovary syndrome, the first years after periods start and the years before the menopause, oestrogen thickens the lining without the progesterone that would normally mature and stabilise it, so there is no orderly withdrawal bleed and the lining is shed late, heavily and unpredictably.

commonCauses.name: Copper intrauterine device
commonCauses.note: The non-hormonal coil often makes periods heavier and longer, particularly in the first few months after it is fitted.

lessCommon.name: Bleeding disorders and anticoagulant medicines
lessCommon.note: Inherited clotting problems such as von Willebrand disease (heavy periods since the very first period, easy bruising, nosebleeds) and anticoagulant medicines increase menstrual loss.

lessCommon.name: Thyroid disease
lessCommon.note: An underactive thyroid can make periods heavier and more frequent, which is why thyroid function is checked when other features suggest it.

lessCommon.name: Endometrial hyperplasia and cancer
lessCommon.note: Overgrowth or cancer of the uterine lining is more likely over 45, with obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome or long gaps between periods, and when heavy periods come with bleeding between periods or after sex; it is investigated with ultrasound of the lining and an endometrial biopsy.

lessCommon.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
lessCommon.note: Infection of the uterus and tubes can cause heavy or irregular bleeding with pelvic pain, unusual discharge and fever.

lessCommon.name: Early pregnancy loss
lessCommon.note: A miscarriage can be mistaken for a late, heavy period with clots, so a pregnancy test is part of the assessment of any unusually heavy bleed.

urgent: Soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for several hours in a row
Bleeding with dizziness, fainting, a racing heartbeat or breathlessness
Heavy bleeding when pregnancy is possible, or after a late or missed period
Heavy bleeding with severe pain, a high temperature or an unusual discharge
Bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, which needs a GP appointment even when it is light

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

pelvic-pain.name: Pelvic pain
pelvic-pain.what: Pain felt low in the abdomen, below the navel and between the hip bones. The pelvis holds the bladder and the lower bowel in everyone, the uterus, ovaries and fallopian tubes in women and anyone with these organs, and the prostate in men and anyone with a prostate, including trans women, all resting on the sling of the pelvic floor muscles. Pain from these organs is often felt in the same place, so its timing (with periods, with passing urine or stool, with sex), whether it is one-sided, and whether a pregnancy is possible do more to point to the cause than the site alone. Pain that lasts six months or more is called chronic pelvic pain; it frequently has more than one contributing cause, including tension in the pelvic floor muscles and sensitised nerves, and is managed differently from a single acute episode.

commonCauses.name: Period pain (primary dysmenorrhoea)
commonCauses.note: Cramping pain in the lower abdomen and back during the first days of a period, caused by the uterus contracting; it usually eases with heat and simple painkillers.

commonCauses.name: Ovulation pain (mittelschmerz)
commonCauses.note: A one-sided ache or sharp twinge around the middle of the cycle, lasting from a few hours to a day or two, as a follicle releases its egg.

commonCauses.name: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.note: A suprapubic ache with burning on passing urine, frequency and urgency, and cloudy or bloody urine.

commonCauses.name: Constipation and irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.note: Cramping, bloating and a change in bowel habit, often relieved by passing stool or wind; irritable bowel syndrome is a common contributor to long-standing pelvic pain.

commonCauses.name: Endometriosis
commonCauses.note: Painful periods that worsen over the years, pain during or after sex, and pain on opening the bowels or passing urine during a period; a common cause of chronic pelvic pain that often takes a long time to diagnose.

commonCauses.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
commonCauses.note: Infection of the uterus, tubes and ovaries, often following a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea, although other bacteria spreading up from the vagina or cervix also cause it, with pain, unusual discharge, bleeding after sex or between periods and sometimes fever; untreated, it can scar the tubes.

lessCommon.name: Ectopic pregnancy
lessCommon.note: A pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube: one-sided pain and light bleeding about six to eight weeks after the last period, with shoulder-tip pain or faintness if the tube ruptures. An emergency.

lessCommon.name: Ovarian cyst torsion or rupture
lessCommon.note: Most ovarian cysts cause no pain, but a cyst that twists on its blood supply or bursts causes sudden, severe one-sided pain, often with vomiting; torsion needs urgent surgery to save the ovary.

lessCommon.name: Appendicitis
lessCommon.note: Pain that starts around the navel and settles in the lower right abdomen, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever; it can be hard to tell from pain in the right ovary or tube.

lessCommon.name: Fibroids
lessCommon.note: Benign growths of the uterine muscle that cause pressure, heaviness and heavy periods, and acute pain if a fibroid outgrows its blood supply or twists.

lessCommon.name: Prostatitis and chronic pelvic pain in men
lessCommon.note: Pain in the perineum, testicles, lower back or penis with urinary symptoms; acute bacterial prostatitis brings fever and feeling very unwell and needs urgent antibiotic treatment, whereas chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men usually has no identified infection.

lessCommon.name: Adhesions and pelvic floor muscle dysfunction
lessCommon.note: Scar tissue after surgery or infection, and pelvic floor muscles that are over-tight or poorly coordinated, can cause persistent deep pain, pain with sex and difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel.

urgent: Pelvic pain with a positive pregnancy test or a missed period, especially with vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or collapse
Sudden, severe pain on one side, particularly with vomiting, a racing pulse or cold, clammy skin
Pain with a high temperature, shivering or an unusual vaginal discharge
Pain with an inability to pass urine, or with blood in the urine

New and persistent bloating, feeling full quickly or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or passing urine more often or more urgently, when these happen on most days (NICE uses more than about 12 times a month), especially at age 50 or over

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

vaginal-bleeding.name: Unusual vaginal bleeding
vaginal-bleeding.what: Bleeding from the vagina at a time when a period is not due: between periods, after sex, after the menopause (once a year has passed since the last period), or during pregnancy. Cervical screening is offered to people without symptoms and is not the test for unusual bleeding: bleeding needs the cervix to be looked at directly. The blood may come from the lining of the uterus, the cervix, the vaginal wall or the vulva, and is occasionally confused with bleeding from the urethra or rectum. Stage of life narrows the causes. In the reproductive years hormonal and infective causes are the commonest, and a pregnancy test is part of every assessment. After the menopause even a single episode of light bleeding is treated as a warning sign: most post-menopausal bleeding turns out to have a benign cause, most often thinning of the lining of the vagina and of the uterus, but it can be the first sign of cancer of the uterine lining, and NICE guidance treats it as a reason for urgent investigation. Trans men and non-binary people with a uterus usually stop having periods on testosterone; bleeding that starts again needs the same assessment.

commonCauses.name: Hormonal contraception
commonCauses.note: Breakthrough bleeding or spotting is common in the first few months of the pill, patch, implant, injection and hormonal coil, and after missed pills; it usually settles, but bleeding that persists is checked for other causes.

commonCauses.name: Irregular ovulation
commonCauses.note: In the first years after periods start, in the years before the menopause and in polycystic ovary syndrome, cycles are unpredictable and bleeding can be irregular, prolonged or arrive between expected periods.

commonCauses.name: Cervical ectropion and polyps
commonCauses.note: Soft glandular cells on the outer surface of the cervix (common in pregnancy and on the pill) and benign polyps of the cervix or uterine lining bleed easily, typically after sex or as spotting between periods.

commonCauses.name: Infection
commonCauses.note: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and pelvic inflammatory disease cause bleeding after sex or between periods, often with discharge, pain or fever; swabs for sexually transmitted infections are part of the assessment.

commonCauses.name: Fibroids
commonCauses.note: Benign growths of the uterine muscle cause heavy, prolonged periods and sometimes bleeding between them.

commonCauses.name: Early pregnancy
commonCauses.note: Light spotting around the time of implantation is common, but bleeding in a known or possible pregnancy can signal a threatened or actual miscarriage and always needs assessment.

lessCommon.name: Ectopic pregnancy
lessCommon.note: Light, often dark bleeding with one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness about six to eight weeks after the last period; a pregnancy outside the uterus can rupture and is an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Cervical cancer
lessCommon.note: Bleeding after sex, between periods or after the menopause, with or without an unusual discharge. Cervical screening is a test for people without symptoms, so bleeding needs the cervix to be examined directly.

lessCommon.name: Cancer of the uterine lining
lessCommon.note: Endometrial cancer most often presents as post-menopausal bleeding and is more likely with obesity, diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome or oestrogen taken without a progestogen; it is investigated with a transvaginal ultrasound of the lining and an endometrial biopsy.

lessCommon.name: Vaginal atrophy and injury
lessCommon.note: Low oestrogen after the menopause, and in trans men on testosterone, thins the vaginal lining so that it bleeds after sex; injury to the vulva or vagina is another cause. Atrophy is settled on as the explanation only once cancer has been excluded.

lessCommon.name: Bleeding disorders and anticoagulant medicines
lessCommon.note: Inherited clotting disorders and anticoagulant medicines make menstrual and other bleeding heavier and more prolonged.

urgent: Heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting, a racing pulse or breathlessness
Bleeding in pregnancy or when pregnancy is possible, especially with one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness
Any bleeding after the menopause, even a single episode of spotting, which needs an urgent GP appointment
Bleeding after sex on more than one occasion, or bleeding between periods that continues for more than a few cycles
Bleeding with pelvic pain, fever or an offensive discharge, or bleeding that returns after periods had stopped on testosterone

coronary-artery-disease.name: Coronary artery disease
coronary-artery-disease.definition: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty plaque (atherosclerosis), limiting blood flow to the heart muscle.
coronary-artery-disease.overview: Plaque builds up over decades in the arteries that supply the heart. When a narrowing limits flow during exertion the muscle becomes short of oxygen and signals this as angina; when a plaque ruptures and a clot blocks the artery, the result is a heart attack. It is the leading cause of death worldwide, and largely preventable.
causes: Atherosclerosis: cholesterol-rich plaque forming in the artery wall, driven by inflammation
riskFactors: Family history of early heart disease
signs: Often none between attacks
Signs of risk factors: high blood pressure, xanthelasma, nicotine staining
coronary-artery-disease.diagnosis: The story of exertional chest pressure relieved by rest is the key. An ECG may be normal at rest; a stress test, CT coronary angiography or invasive angiography shows the narrowings. Blood tests assess cholesterol, glucose and kidney function.
coronary-artery-disease.treatment: Lifestyle change and medication for everyone: stop smoking, statins to lower LDL, aspirin to prevent clots, blood pressure and diabetes control, and drugs to relieve angina (nitrates, beta blockers). Significant narrowings can be opened with angioplasty and a stent or bypassed with surgery.
coronary-artery-disease.prevention: Not smoking, regular exercise, a diet low in saturated fat and salt, healthy weight, and treating blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
coronary-artery-disease.seekCare: Call emergency services for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, or angina that is new, more frequent or occurs at rest.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

myocardial-infarction.name: Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
myocardial-infarction.definition: Death of heart muscle because a coronary artery is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot forming on a ruptured plaque.
myocardial-infarction.overview: Every minute of blockage kills more muscle, so a heart attack is treated as a race to reopen the artery. Survival and the amount of muscle saved depend on how quickly the person calls for help and reaches a hospital able to perform emergency angioplasty.
causes: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with clot formation
Less often: coronary spasm, spontaneous artery dissection, severe anaemia or oxygen lack with a fixed narrowing
riskFactors: Same as coronary artery disease: smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes, family history, age
signs: Pale, sweaty, distressed
Fast or slow pulse, low or high blood pressure
Crackles in the lungs if the heart is failing
complications: Rupture of the heart wall or a papillary muscle
myocardial-infarction.diagnosis: An ECG within ten minutes of arrival shows ST elevation (STEMI) when a large artery is fully blocked; troponin in the blood rises over hours and confirms muscle damage in other cases. Echocardiography shows which wall has stopped moving.
myocardial-infarction.treatment: Aspirin immediately, then emergency angioplasty with a stent to reopen the artery (or clot-dissolving drugs if angioplasty is not reachable within about two hours). Afterwards: a second antiplatelet drug, a statin, a beta blocker and an ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehabilitation and risk factor control.
myocardial-infarction.prevention: The measures that prevent coronary artery disease; after a first attack, lifelong medication and rehabilitation halve the risk of another.
myocardial-infarction.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately for crushing chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or chest discomfort with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Do not drive yourself.
