vitamin-d.name: Vitamin D test
vitamin-d.what: Measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form the liver makes from vitamin D obtained from sunlight on skin and from food or supplements. It is the best single measure of vitamin D status and is used when bone pain, muscle weakness, osteoporosis, malabsorption or a low calcium make deficiency likely.

measures.meaning: The circulating storage form, reflecting weeks of sun exposure and intake; the kidney converts it to the active hormone that raises calcium absorption.

whyOrdered: Bone pain, muscle weakness or unexplained fatigue when deficiency is suspected
Osteoporosis, fractures and before starting bone treatments
Low calcium or a raised alkaline phosphatase or parathyroid hormone
Conditions that impair absorption: coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, after bariatric surgery
Chronic kidney disease and some other long-term conditions

interpretation.meaning: Levels at which bone softening (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults) becomes likely; treatment with vitamin D is usually given
Below the level considered adequate for bone health; supplementation is often advised, particularly in groups at risk
Sufficient for bone health in most people
Usually from excess supplements; can cause a high calcium and is reviewed

vitamin-d.rangeNote: Vitamin D is read against widely used cut-offs for deficiency, insufficiency and adequacy that differ slightly between countries and professional bodies, not against a population reference interval. The laboratory reports the cut-offs it applies, and the assay method affects the value.
factors: Season and latitude: levels fall in winter and in people who cover their skin or stay indoors
Skin pigmentation, age and body weight
Supplements and fortified foods
Liver and kidney disease, which affect the conversion of vitamin D
The assay method, which changes results between laboratories
cannotTell: Bone density, which needs a DXA scan
Whether symptoms are caused by the deficiency, which is common and often coincidental
The active hormone level (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), a separate test used only in specific disorders
vitamin-d.limitations: Population screening is not recommended; the test is for people with symptoms or risk factors. Assays vary and the value moves with the seasons, so a single result is interpreted with the time of year and the person's circumstances.
vitamin-d.medicinesNote: Vitamin D supplements raise it; some antiepileptics, glucocorticoids, orlistat and cholestyramine lower it.

quick.usedFor: Suspected vitamin D deficiency, bone disease, malabsorption, before bone treatments
quick.measures: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form of vitamin D

vitamin-d.resultType: Numeric, read against deficiency and adequacy cut-offs

references.title: NICE TA464: Bisphosphonates for treating osteoporosis

components.name: 25-hydroxyvitamin D
components.measures: The storage form of vitamin D
components.high: Excess supplements
components.low: Little sunlight, low intake, malabsorption, kidney or liver disease

hepatitis-b-serology.name: Hepatitis B tests
hepatitis-b-serology.what: A set of blood tests that shows whether someone has hepatitis B now, had it in the past, is immune from vaccination, or carries the virus long term. Each marker answers a different question: the surface antigen shows current infection, the antibodies show immunity or past exposure, and the viral DNA measures how actively the virus is multiplying.

measures.meaning: Part of the virus's outer coat; present in acute and chronic infection. Persisting beyond six months defines chronic hepatitis B.
The protective antibody; present after vaccination or recovered infection.
Marks exposure to the virus at some time; absent after vaccination alone. The IgM form points to recent infection.

measures.item: e antigen and e antibody (HBeAg, anti-HBe)
measures.meaning: Indicate how actively the virus is replicating in chronic infection.
The amount of virus in the blood, measured by PCR; guides the decision to treat and shows whether treatment is working.

whyOrdered: Abnormal liver tests or symptoms of hepatitis
Screening in pregnancy, before immunosuppressive treatment, and in people at higher risk
After a possible exposure, such as a needlestick injury
Checking immunity after vaccination
Monitoring chronic hepatitis B and its treatment
hepatitis-b-serology.how: A venous blood sample; the laboratory runs the markers as a panel and adds viral DNA when the surface antigen is positive.

interpretation.meaning: Current infection, acute or chronic; further markers and liver assessment follow, and specialist care is arranged
Immunity from vaccination

interpretation.finding: anti-HBs and anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative
interpretation.meaning: Past infection that has resolved, with immunity

interpretation.finding: HBsAg positive for more than six months
interpretation.meaning: Chronic hepatitis B; the viral load, e-antigen status and liver tests decide on monitoring and antiviral treatment
Never infected and not immune; vaccination is considered

hepatitis-b-serology.rangeNote: Antigen and antibody results are reported as positive or negative (with a level for anti-HBs after vaccination); the viral load is a number whose meaning depends on the clinical context and the treatment guidelines in use, not on a reference interval.
factors: Timing after exposure: markers appear in sequence over weeks
Recent vaccination, which produces anti-HBs only
Immunosuppression, which can reactivate a resolved infection
Very early or 'window period' infection, when only anti-HBc IgM may be positive
cannotTell: How much liver damage has occurred, which needs liver tests, elastography or biopsy
Whether hepatitis C, D or other liver diseases are also present without their own tests
Exactly when the infection was acquired
hepatitis-b-serology.limitations: The markers must be read as a pattern; a single result can mislead in the window period, after vaccination or in people with weak immunity. Chronic infection needs long-term specialist monitoring even when the person feels well.
hepatitis-b-serology.medicinesNote: Antiviral treatment for hepatitis B lowers the viral load; the test monitors that treatment. Immunosuppressive medicines can reactivate the virus, so screening is done before they are started.

quick.usedFor: Diagnosing and monitoring hepatitis B, checking immunity, screening in pregnancy and before immunosuppression
quick.measures: Hepatitis B antigens, antibodies and viral DNA

hepatitis-b-serology.resultType: Positive or negative markers read as a pattern, plus a viral load

hiv-test.name: HIV test
hiv-test.what: A blood test that looks for the human immunodeficiency virus, usually by detecting both a viral protein (p24 antigen) and the antibodies the immune system makes against the virus. Modern combined tests become positive within a few weeks of infection; a positive screening result is always confirmed with a second test before a diagnosis is given.

measures.item: HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies with p24 antigen
measures.meaning: The standard fourth-generation laboratory screen, reliable from about 45 days after exposure; antigen detection shortens the window.
Fingerprick or saliva tests with results in minutes; a reactive result must be confirmed by a laboratory.

measures.item: HIV RNA (viral load) and CD4 count
measures.meaning: After diagnosis: the amount of virus and the number of CD4 immune cells, used to plan and monitor treatment rather than to screen.

whyOrdered: Routine screening: HIV testing is offered widely because early treatment protects health and prevents transmission
After a possible exposure, at the right interval
Symptoms of seroconversion or of an immune system under attack
Pregnancy screening, before some treatments and in people diagnosed with other sexually transmitted infections
hiv-test.how: A venous blood sample in a laboratory, a fingerprick rapid test in a clinic or pharmacy, or a home self-test kit.
hiv-test.preparation: None. The window period matters: a test taken too soon after exposure can be negative, so a repeat at the recommended interval may be advised.

interpretation.meaning: HIV infection is very unlikely; repeat testing is advised after any further exposure
Possible infection; a confirmatory laboratory test on a new sample is done before any diagnosis
HIV infection; referral to specialist care, where viral load and CD4 count guide antiretroviral treatment that keeps the virus suppressed
Inconclusive; the test is repeated at the interval recommended for the type of test used

hiv-test.rangeNote: Screening results are reported as negative or reactive, and confirmed positive or negative; no numeric reference interval applies. Viral load and CD4 count after diagnosis are numbers interpreted against treatment guidelines.
factors: The interval since exposure (window period), which depends on the test type
Post-exposure or pre-exposure prophylaxis medicines, which can delay antibody development
Rare false-reactive screening results, which is why confirmation is required
cannotTell: Whether infection occurred within the last few weeks, before markers appear
The stage of infection or the state of the immune system, which need the viral load and CD4 count
Other sexually transmitted infections, which have their own tests
hiv-test.limitations: No test detects infection immediately after exposure; results are only interpreted in relation to the timing of exposure, and a screening result is never a diagnosis on its own. Self-tests carry the same window-period limits and need confirmation.
hiv-test.medicinesNote: Antiretroviral prophylaxis can delay or blunt antibody responses; antiretroviral treatment lowers the viral load, which the monitoring tests track.

quick.type: Blood test (serology; rapid and self-tests available)
quick.sample: Blood from a vein, a fingerprick, or saliva for self-tests
quick.usedFor: Screening for HIV, testing after exposure, monitoring treatment once diagnosed
quick.measures: HIV antibodies and p24 antigen; viral load and CD4 count after diagnosis

hiv-test.specimen: Venous blood (serum) in the laboratory; capillary blood or oral fluid for rapid and self-tests
hiv-test.resultType: Negative, reactive or confirmed positive; numeric viral load and CD4 count in monitoring

references.title: WHO: HIV and AIDS fact sheet

blood-pressure-measurement.name: Blood pressure measurement
blood-pressure-measurement.what: The pressure of blood against the artery walls, recorded as two numbers: the systolic pressure when the heart contracts and the diastolic pressure between beats. Measured with a cuff on the upper arm, it is the most frequently taken measurement in medicine because raised blood pressure usually causes no symptoms yet drives heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease.

measures.meaning: The peak pressure as the left ventricle ejects blood, in mmHg.
The lowest pressure, while the heart refills, in mmHg.
Readings taken automatically over 24 hours by a worn cuff; the daytime average is the reference measurement for diagnosing hypertension.
Twice-daily readings taken by the person over several days with a validated arm cuff, averaged.

whyOrdered: Routine health checks and screening for hypertension
Confirming a raised clinic reading with ambulatory or home monitoring
Monitoring blood-pressure treatment
Dizziness on standing, when lying and standing readings are compared
In pregnancy, kidney disease, diabetes and after a stroke or heart attack
blood-pressure-measurement.how: Seated and rested for a few minutes, arm supported at heart level, a correctly sized cuff on the upper arm; readings are repeated and the average used. Ambulatory monitoring uses an automatic cuff worn for 24 hours; home monitoring uses a validated upper-arm device morning and evening for several days.
blood-pressure-measurement.preparation: Avoid caffeine, smoking and exercise for 30 minutes before; empty the bladder; sit quietly with the back supported and legs uncrossed; do not talk during the reading.

interpretation.meaning: Hypertension is suspected but not diagnosed: ambulatory or home monitoring confirms it, because clinic readings are often higher than usual (white-coat effect)

interpretation.finding: Ambulatory or home average above the diagnostic threshold
interpretation.meaning: Hypertension; the stage, cardiovascular risk and any organ damage guide lifestyle advice and treatment
Severe hypertension or an emergency; assessed the same day
Postural (orthostatic) hypotension, a common cause of dizziness and falls, often from medicines or dehydration

blood-pressure-measurement.rangeNote: Blood pressure is read against guideline thresholds for diagnosis and treatment targets, which differ between clinic, ambulatory and home readings and between countries' guidelines; it is not read against a laboratory reference interval.

thresholds.name: Clinic blood pressure suggesting hypertension
thresholds.context: A clinic reading at or above this prompts ambulatory (or home) monitoring to confirm the diagnosis

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management
source.section: 1.2 Measuring blood pressure and 1.3 Diagnosing hypertension

thresholds.name: Ambulatory or home average confirming stage 1 hypertension
thresholds.context: Diagnosis of stage 1 hypertension when the clinic reading is 140/90 or higher

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

thresholds.name: Stage 2 hypertension
thresholds.context: Treatment is offered to adults of any age with stage 2 hypertension

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

factors: Cuff size, arm position, talking, a full bladder and recent caffeine, smoking or exercise
The clinic setting itself (white-coat effect) and, conversely, masked hypertension that is normal in clinic but raised at home
Pain, anxiety, cold and the time of day
Medicines: decongestants, NSAIDs, steroids, oral contraceptives and stimulants raise it; antihypertensives, some antidepressants and alcohol change it
cannotTell: Whether arteries or organs have been damaged, which needs blood tests, urine tests, an ECG and sometimes imaging
The cause of high blood pressure, which is usually not identifiable and occasionally due to kidney, adrenal or other disease
Blood pressure inside the heart or lungs, which needs catheter studies
blood-pressure-measurement.limitations: A single reading is a poor guide: blood pressure varies minute to minute, and diagnosis rests on averaged out-of-clinic readings. Wrist and finger devices are less reliable than validated upper-arm cuffs, and irregular rhythms such as atrial fibrillation make automatic devices inaccurate.
blood-pressure-measurement.medicinesNote: Antihypertensive medicines are what the measurement monitors; NSAIDs, decongestants, corticosteroids and some antidepressants can raise it.

quick.sample: None: a cuff on the upper arm
quick.usedFor: Screening for and diagnosing hypertension, monitoring treatment, assessing dizziness on standing
quick.measures: Systolic and diastolic arterial pressure in mmHg

blood-pressure-measurement.resultType: Two numbers in mmHg, read against guideline thresholds; averaged home or ambulatory readings for diagnosis

cervical-screening.name: Cervical screening (smear test)
cervical-screening.what: A sample of cells brushed from the transformation zone of the cervix, the band where the columnar lining of the cervical canal has been replaced by squamous cells and where nearly all cervical cell changes begin, taken with a small soft brush passed through a speculum. In England the sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus behind almost all cervical cancer, and the cells are examined under the microscope only if that virus is found. Screening looks for the risk of cancer developing rather than for cancer itself, and it is offered to everyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people.

measures.meaning: The virus types that cause cervical cancer, chiefly types 16 and 18. A negative result means the chance of cancer developing before the next screen is very low.
Looked at only when high-risk HPV is found. Cells are reported as normal, borderline, or as low-grade or high-grade dyskaryosis, according to how abnormal they appear.
A sample with too few cells, or obscured by blood or inflammation, is reported as inadequate and has to be repeated.

whyOrdered: Routine screening for everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 in England, at intervals that depend on age, the previous result and the programme (the four UK nations differ)
A repeat a year after a high-risk HPV result with normal cells, to see whether the infection has cleared
Follow-up after treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), as a test of cure
Trans men and non-binary people who have a cervix: those registered with a GP as male are not sent automatic invitations and need to ask for screening
Not for investigating symptoms: bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause needs an examination of the cervix and referral, not a screening test
cervical-screening.how: A speculum is passed into the vagina so that the cervix can be seen, and a small soft brush is rotated in the opening of the cervix for a few seconds. The tip of the brush is put into a pot of preservative liquid and sent to the laboratory (liquid-based cytology). The appointment takes a few minutes and is usually done by a practice nurse.
cervical-screening.preparation: None is needed, although it is better not to book during a period because blood makes the sample harder to read, and vaginal medicines, lubricants and spermicides are avoided for a couple of days beforehand. A test that falls due in pregnancy is usually put off, and screening is normally taken up again about twelve weeks after giving birth; anyone who is pregnant and has been invited should say so when booking. Discomfort and anxiety can be reduced by asking for a smaller speculum, a different position or a longer appointment, and a course of vaginal oestrogen is sometimes prescribed first when the tissues are thin after the menopause or on testosterone.

interpretation.meaning: Routine recall; the chance of cervical cancer developing before the next invitation is very low
Screening is repeated in a year, because most infections clear on their own

interpretation.finding: High-risk HPV found with abnormal cells
interpretation.meaning: Referral for colposcopy: the cervix is examined under magnification and a biopsy or loop excision may be taken

interpretation.finding: High-risk HPV still present on repeat testing
interpretation.meaning: Screening is repeated after a further year; high-risk HPV that is still present at that second repeat leads to colposcopy even when the cells look normal, because it is persistent infection that leads to cancer
Repeated after about three months; repeated inadequate samples lead to colposcopy

cervical-screening.limitations: Screening lowers the risk of cervical cancer a great deal but does not remove it. HPV vaccination protects against the commonest high-risk types but not all of them, so screening invitations still apply to people who have been vaccinated. A sample can miss an abnormal area, and adenocarcinoma arising high in the cervical canal is harder to detect than squamous disease. A positive HPV result is common, says nothing about when or from whom the virus was acquired, and in most people clears without treatment within about two years. The test says nothing about the ovaries, the lining of the uterus or other infections, and it cannot be used to investigate bleeding or pain, which need an examination. Kits for taking a sample at home are being introduced in some programmes for people who do not attend.

meta.name: Imaging
meta.about: Imaging studies: how each modality works, what it shows well and badly, radiation and preparation. Educational, not a guide to which scan an individual should have.

x-ray.name: X-ray
x-ray.summary: The oldest and most widely available imaging test: a brief beam of X-rays casts a shadow picture of bone, air and soft tissue, ideal for fractures, chest infections and dental checks.
x-ray.how: A brief pulse of X-rays passes through the body onto a digital detector. Dense tissue such as bone absorbs most of the beam and appears white; air absorbs almost none and appears black; soft tissue and fluid are shades of grey in between. The image is a two-dimensional shadow of everything in the beam's path.
shows: Bone: fractures, dislocations, arthritis, bone tumours and infection
Chest: pneumonia, fluid, collapsed lung, heart size, tumours
Abdomen: bowel obstruction, free air from a perforation, some stones
Teeth and jaw
Foreign bodies made of metal or glass
bestFor: A first look at bones and the chest: fast, cheap and available everywhere
Following fracture healing
Bowel obstruction and perforation as a screen
notFor: Soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage, brain and spinal cord
Early stress fractures and small bone injuries (MRI or CT)
Subtle lung disease (CT)
x-ray.preparation: None. Remove metal from the area; tell the radiographer about any possibility of pregnancy.
x-ray.duration: A few minutes; the exposure lasts a fraction of a second.
x-ray.dose: A chest X-ray is about 0.1 mSv, comparable to a few days of natural background radiation; a lumbar spine film is around 1 mSv.
x-ray.risks: The radiation dose is tiny for a single film; the abdomen and pelvis are shielded or avoided in pregnancy unless essential.
x-ray.contrast: Barium swallows and enemas coat the gut to outline it on fluoroscopy; iodine contrast is used for joints (arthrogram) and blood vessels (angiography).

commonUses.use: Cough, breathlessness, chest pain, fever, suspected pneumonia or heart failure
Injury, joint pain, suspected fracture, osteoarthritis
Obstruction, perforation, swallowed objects
DEXA scanning uses two low-energy X-ray beams to measure bone mineral density for osteoporosis

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

ct-scan.name: CT scan
ct-scan.summary: A rotating X-ray tube and computer build cross-sectional slices of the body in seconds, showing bone, organs, blood vessels and bleeding in fine detail; the workhorse of emergency imaging.
ct-scan.how: An X-ray tube spins around the body while it moves through the ring, collecting thousands of projections that a computer reconstructs into thin cross-sectional slices. The slices are stacked to view any plane or a 3D model. Iodine contrast injected into a vein lights up blood vessels and shows how organs and tumours take up blood.
shows: Brain: bleeding, stroke (once established), tumours, injury
Chest: lung nodules and cancer, blood clots in the lung arteries (CTPA), fibrosis, infection
Abdomen and pelvis: appendicitis, diverticulitis, kidney stones, tumours, abscesses, bowel obstruction
Bones: complex fractures, the spine and pelvis
Blood vessels: aneurysms, dissection, coronary artery narrowing (CT coronary angiography)
bestFor: Emergencies where speed matters: trauma, stroke, suspected bleeding, severe abdominal pain
Lung disease and cancer staging
Kidney stones (no contrast needed)
Detailed bone anatomy for surgical planning
notFor: Early stroke (may look normal for hours), spinal cord, ligaments and cartilage (MRI)
Repeated scans in children and young adults where dose accumulates
People with severe kidney disease or contrast allergy (contrast may be withheld)
ct-scan.preparation: Fasting for a few hours before contrast; kidney function checked; a cannula placed. Oral contrast is sometimes drunk an hour before abdominal scans.
ct-scan.duration: The scan itself takes seconds to a few minutes; the visit 20-30 minutes.
ct-scan.dose: A head CT is about 2 mSv, a chest CT 5-7 mSv and an abdomen-pelvis CT around 10 mSv: several years of background radiation, though modern scanners use far less than older ones.
ct-scan.risks: A small increase in lifetime cancer risk with each scan, weighed against the benefit; contrast reactions (rare) and a temporary drop in kidney function in those already at risk. Avoided in pregnancy unless essential.
ct-scan.contrast: Iodine-based, injected into a vein for vessels, organs and tumours; causes a warm flush and a metallic taste. Metformin may be paused around the scan.

commonUses.use: Head injury, sudden severe headache, first seizure, suspected stroke or bleed
Lung cancer staging, pulmonary embolism (CTPA), fibrosis, complicated pneumonia
Severe pain, suspected appendicitis, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, cancer staging
CT coronary angiography for stable chest pain; calcium scoring

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

mri.name: MRI scan
mri.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not radiation, to produce detailed pictures of soft tissue: the brain, spinal cord, joints, muscles and organs.
mri.how: A powerful magnet aligns the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat. Radio pulses knock them out of alignment and, as they relax back, they emit faint signals that differ by tissue type. Different pulse sequences (T1, T2, diffusion, fat suppression) emphasise different properties, giving unrivalled soft-tissue contrast without ionising radiation.
shows: Brain and spinal cord: stroke within minutes (diffusion), multiple sclerosis, tumours, epilepsy foci, dementia patterns
Spine: disc herniation, nerve compression, infection, cord injury
Joints: cartilage, menisci, ligaments, tendons, bone marrow oedema (early stress fractures)
Heart: muscle scar, cardiomyopathy, congenital disease
Liver, pancreas, bile ducts (MRCP), prostate, pelvis, breast
bestFor: Any question about the brain, spinal cord or nerves
Ligament, cartilage and tendon injuries of the knee, shoulder and ankle
Characterising liver, pancreatic and prostate lesions
Children and pregnancy, where radiation is avoided
notFor: Emergencies needing speed (a scan takes 20-60 minutes and the environment is hard to monitor)
Lungs and calcified structures (few hydrogen nuclei; CT is better)
People with certain implants, severe claustrophobia, or who cannot lie still
mri.preparation: A detailed safety questionnaire about implants, metal fragments, pacemakers and previous surgery; all metal removed; ear protection for the loud knocking. Fasting for some abdominal scans.
mri.duration: 20-60 minutes lying still inside a tube; each sequence lasts a few minutes.
mri.dose: No ionising radiation; the magnetic field and radio waves have no known lasting effect at diagnostic strengths.
mri.risks: Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles; older pacemakers, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and metal in the eye can be dangerous. Gadolinium contrast is avoided in severe kidney disease and pregnancy. Claustrophobia is the commonest problem.
mri.contrast: Gadolinium, injected into a vein, highlights tumours, inflammation and blood vessels; rare allergic reactions.

commonUses.use: Stroke, tumours, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, dementia, headache with red flags
Sciatica with weakness, suspected cauda equina, infection, myelopathy
Ligament and meniscal tears, rotator cuff tears, cartilage
Liver lesions, bile duct stones (MRCP), prostate cancer, endometriosis, rectal cancer staging

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

ultrasound.name: Ultrasound
ultrasound.summary: High-frequency sound waves bounced off tissue give real-time, radiation-free images, used for pregnancy, the abdomen, the heart (echocardiography), blood vessels and guiding needles.
ultrasound.how: A hand-held probe sends pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes from tissue boundaries. The depth of each echo builds a live moving image. Doppler ultrasound measures the frequency shift from moving blood to show flow direction and speed in colour. It is safe, portable and real-time, but sound cannot cross bone or air.
shows: Abdomen: gallstones, liver size and texture, kidney obstruction, aortic aneurysm, fluid
Pelvis: pregnancy, ovaries and uterus, bladder volume, prostate (transrectal)
Vessels: deep vein thrombosis, carotid narrowing, varicose veins, arterial blockages
Heart: the echocardiogram
Soft tissue: thyroid nodules, breast lumps, lymph nodes, tendons, muscle tears, abscesses
Guidance for needles: biopsies, drains, injections, cannulas
bestFor: First test for the gallbladder, kidneys, thyroid, scrotum, pregnancy and leg veins
Any test that must be repeated or done at the bedside
Guiding procedures in real time
Children and pregnancy
notFor: Anything behind bone (brain in adults, spinal cord) or air (lungs beyond the surface, gas-filled bowel)
Deep structures in larger patients (image quality falls with depth)
A comprehensive survey: it shows what the operator points at, so quality depends on skill
ultrasound.preparation: Fasting for gallbladder scans so it is full; a full bladder for pelvic scans; otherwise none.
ultrasound.dose: No ionising radiation; diagnostic ultrasound has no known harmful effects at the energies used.
ultrasound.risks: None known; brief discomfort from probe pressure on a tender area.
ultrasound.contrast: Microbubble contrast (tiny gas bubbles injected into a vein) improves characterisation of liver and kidney lesions.

commonUses.use: Gallstones, jaundice, abnormal liver tests
Early pregnancy and its location, fibroids, ovarian cysts, the endometrium after bleeding; transvaginal for detail
Kidney injury, obstruction, stones, bladder emptying
Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Thyroid nodules, lymph nodes, carotid stenosis after a stroke
Tendon tears, joint effusions, guiding steroid injections

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

pet-scan.name: PET-CT scan
pet-scan.summary: Positron emission tomography tracks a mildly radioactive sugar or tracer to show where cells are most active, usually combined with CT to stage cancer and check treatment response.
pet-scan.how: A tiny amount of a radioactive tracer is injected and the scanner detects where it accumulates. The commonest tracer, FDG, is a glucose analogue, so tissues that burn a lot of sugar (most cancers, infection, inflammation, the brain and heart) light up. The PET image is fused with a CT taken at the same time to show exactly where the activity sits. Other nuclear medicine scans use tracers that go to bone, the thyroid, the heart muscle or the kidneys.
shows: Cancer: staging, finding spread, judging response to treatment, distinguishing scar from active tumour
Infection and inflammation of unknown source, vasculitis, infected grafts
Brain: dementia patterns, epilepsy foci
Heart: viable versus scarred muscle
Bone scan: metastases, stress fractures, infection, Paget disease
Thyroid uptake scan: overactive nodules versus thyroiditis
bestFor: Whole-body cancer staging in lung cancer, lymphoma, melanoma, oesophageal and head and neck cancer
Deciding whether a lung nodule is likely malignant
Fever of unknown origin
notFor: Cancers with low glucose uptake (some prostate, kidney, low-grade tumours; other tracers are used)
Small lesions under about 5 mm
Brain metastases (the brain glows with normal uptake; MRI instead)
Uncontrolled diabetes, which spoils FDG uptake
pet-scan.preparation: Fast for 6 hours, avoid exercise for 24 hours, keep warm; blood glucose checked. Sit quietly for an hour after injection while the tracer distributes.
pet-scan.duration: About 2-3 hours in the department; scanning 20-30 minutes.
pet-scan.dose: Around 7 mSv from the tracer plus the CT component, in total roughly 10-25 mSv depending on protocol.
pet-scan.risks: Radiation as above; avoid close contact with pregnant women and small children for a few hours after the tracer. No allergic risk from FDG.
pet-scan.contrast: The radiotracer itself; the CT component may be low-dose without contrast or a full diagnostic scan with iodine.

commonUses.use: Staging and restaging cancer, planning radiotherapy
Characterising a lung nodule; mediastinal lymph nodes
Frontotemporal versus Alzheimer dementia; amyloid PET
Bone scan for metastases or occult fracture

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

mammography.name: Mammography
mammography.summary: A low-dose X-ray of the compressed breast that can detect cancers years before they can be felt, used for screening programmes and for investigating breast symptoms.
mammography.how: A low-dose X-ray of each breast, compressed between two plates for a few seconds to spread the tissue thin and hold it still. Two views are taken of each side. Digital tomosynthesis takes a sweep of images to reconstruct thin slices, reducing overlap. Cancers show as masses, distortions or clusters of tiny calcifications, often years before they can be felt.
shows: Breast cancer, including ductal carcinoma in situ (calcifications)
Benign lumps: cysts, fibroadenomas (with ultrasound to tell them apart)
Breast density, which affects both risk and how easily cancers are seen
bestFor: Population screening of women aged roughly 50-70, every 2-3 years depending on country

Investigating a new lump, nipple change or skin change in women over 40; trans women on long-term oestrogen and trans men who have not had chest surgery are offered screening on the same basis as the tissue they have
Follow-up after breast cancer treatment
notFor: Younger women with dense breasts, where ultrasound and MRI see more
Assessing implants (MRI)
Ruling out cancer completely: about 1 in 8 cancers is missed, so a new lump is always investigated even after a normal screen
mammography.preparation: No deodorant or talc on the day (they mimic calcifications); book after a period if breasts are tender.
mammography.duration: About 10-15 minutes, with each compression lasting a few seconds.
mammography.dose: About 0.4 mSv for two views of both breasts, similar to seven weeks of natural background radiation.
mammography.risks: Discomfort from compression; a small radiation dose; false alarms leading to recalls and biopsies; overdiagnosis of cancers that would never have caused harm.
mammography.contrast: Contrast-enhanced mammography with iodine is an emerging alternative to breast MRI.

commonUses.use: Asymptomatic women in the screening age range
Lump, discharge, dimpling, in a one-stop clinic with examination, ultrasound and needle biopsy
Earlier and yearly screening for BRCA carriers, usually with MRI

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

fluoroscopy.name: Fluoroscopy and angiography
fluoroscopy.summary: Continuous, low-dose X-ray imaging shown as a live moving picture, used to watch swallowing, guide catheters and joint injections and follow contrast through the gut or vessels.
fluoroscopy.how: A continuous or pulsed X-ray beam produces a moving image on a screen, so the radiologist can watch swallowing, bowel movement, joint motion or the passage of contrast through blood vessels in real time. Angiography injects iodine contrast through a fine catheter threaded into an artery, mapping the vessel tree and allowing treatment (angioplasty, stents, coiling, clot removal) in the same session.
shows: Swallowing problems and reflux (barium or water-soluble swallow)
Bowel narrowing, fistulas, leaks after surgery
Blood vessel narrowing, blockage, aneurysms and bleeding points
Coronary arteries during cardiac catheterisation
Guiding the placement of tubes, lines, stents and orthopaedic hardware
bestFor: Anything that must be watched moving
Combining diagnosis and treatment in one sitting (interventional radiology and cardiology)
Checking that a catheter, wire or stent is in the right place
notFor: Routine diagnosis where a still image will do (X-ray, CT) because screening time adds dose
People who cannot cooperate with swallowing or positioning instructions
fluoroscopy.preparation: Fasting for gut studies and angiography; kidney function and clotting checked; blood thinners managed; a cannula for sedation.
fluoroscopy.duration: From 10 minutes for a swallow to 1-3 hours for complex interventional procedures.
fluoroscopy.dose: Highly variable: a barium swallow around 1.5 mSv, a diagnostic coronary angiogram about 7 mSv, long interventions much more. Skin can be injured after very prolonged screening.
fluoroscopy.risks: Radiation dose that rises with screening time; contrast reactions and kidney strain; for angiography, bleeding or damage at the artery puncture site, and rarely stroke or vessel injury.
fluoroscopy.contrast: Barium for the gut (or a water-soluble alternative if a leak is suspected); iodine for vessels, joints and the urinary tract.

commonUses.use: Coronary angiography for heart attack and angina, with angioplasty and stenting
Cerebral angiography for aneurysms; mechanical thrombectomy in stroke
Barium swallow for dysphagia; contrast studies after bowel surgery
Peripheral angiography and angioplasty for blocked leg arteries

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

dxa-scan.name: DXA scan (bone density)
dxa-scan.summary: A quick, very low-dose X-ray measurement of bone mineral density at the hip and spine, reported as a T-score, that diagnoses osteoporosis and estimates fracture risk.
dxa-scan.how: Two X-ray beams of different energies pass through the bone; the difference in how much each is absorbed gives the amount of mineral per area of bone. The scanner passes over the lower spine and hip while the person lies still on a padded table for about 10-20 minutes.
shows: Bone mineral density at the hip and lumbar spine, and sometimes the forearm
A T-score comparing the result with young healthy adults and a Z-score comparing it with people of the same age and sex
Change in density on repeat scans, to monitor treatment
bestFor: Diagnosing osteoporosis and osteopenia
Estimating fracture risk together with clinical risk factors (FRAX)
Deciding on and monitoring bone-protective treatment
Assessing bone loss from long-term corticosteroids or other causes
notFor: Finding the cause of bone or back pain
Detecting fractures, tumours or arthritis in detail: X-ray, CT or MRI do that
Children and people with spinal hardware, where interpretation needs specialist adjustment
dxa-scan.preparation: No calcium supplements on the day of the scan; wear clothes without metal; mention recent contrast X-rays or nuclear scans, which can interfere.
dxa-scan.dose: Very low: a fraction of a chest X-ray, less than a day of natural background radiation.
dxa-scan.risks: Minimal radiation exposure; not done in pregnancy unless essential.

commonUses.use: Bone density for osteoporosis diagnosis and fracture risk
When hip or spine cannot be measured, or in hyperparathyroidism
Body composition (fat and lean mass) in specialist settings

references.title: NICE TA464: Bisphosphonates for treating osteoporosis

meta.name: Procedures
meta.about: Common procedures and operations: why they are done, what happens, recovery and risks, linked to the anatomy involved. Educational; individual advice comes from the treating team.

categories.name: Operations
categories.summary: Procedures done under anaesthetic in an operating theatre.

categories.name: Heart procedures
categories.summary: Catheter and surgical treatments for the heart and coronary arteries.

categories.name: Endoscopic procedures
categories.summary: Looking and treating inside the body through a scope.

categories.name: Bedside procedures
categories.summary: Procedures done in clinic or on the ward with local anaesthetic or none.

appendectomy.name: Appendicectomy
appendectomy.what: Removal of the inflamed appendix, the blind-ended tube hanging off the caecum at the start of the large intestine. Usually done through three small keyhole incisions with a camera (laparoscopically), occasionally through a single cut in the right lower abdomen.
why: Acute appendicitis, to prevent perforation and peritonitis
An appendix mass or abscess after initial antibiotics and drainage
Occasionally, an appendix tumour found on imaging or during other surgery
before: Blood tests, pregnancy test in women, sometimes ultrasound or CT
Nil by mouth; intravenous fluids and antibiotics
Consent and marking; general anaesthetic
steps: Carbon dioxide inflates the abdomen through a port at the navel to create working space
A camera and two instruments are introduced through 5-12 mm ports
The appendix is lifted, its blood supply in the mesoappendix sealed, and its base tied or stapled at the caecum
The appendix is removed in a bag; any pus is washed out
Ports are removed and the small wounds closed with dissolvable stitches
after: Home the same or next day for uncomplicated cases
Simple painkillers; walk early
Antibiotics continued for a few days if the appendix had perforated
appendectomy.recovery: Back to desk work in about a week and to sport in two to four weeks after keyhole surgery; longer after open surgery or a perforated appendix.
risks: Wound infection (more after perforation)
Pelvic abscess
Bleeding, injury to bowel or bladder (rare)
Stump leak, adhesions, hernia at the port site (rare)
Anaesthetic risks
alternatives: Antibiotics alone for uncomplicated appendicitis: works in most short term, but about a third need surgery within a few years
Drainage and delayed surgery for an abscess

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

cholecystectomy.name: Cholecystectomy
cholecystectomy.what: Removal of the gallbladder, the small sac under the liver that stores bile. The commonest planned abdominal operation, almost always done by keyhole surgery. The liver keeps making bile, which then flows straight into the duodenum.
why: Gallstones causing repeated pain (biliary colic)
Acute cholecystitis (an inflamed, infected gallbladder)
Gallstone pancreatitis, once recovered, to prevent recurrence
Gallbladder polyps above 10 mm or a porcelain gallbladder (cancer risk)
before: Ultrasound confirming stones; liver function tests; MRCP or ERCP if stones are suspected in the bile duct
Fasting; general anaesthetic
Antibiotics at induction if inflamed
steps: Four ports: one at the navel for the camera, three under the right ribs
The gallbladder is retracted upward to expose Calot's triangle
The cystic duct and cystic artery are identified with a 'critical view of safety', clipped and divided
The gallbladder is peeled off the liver bed with diathermy and removed in a bag through the navel port
An X-ray of the bile duct (cholangiogram) may be done during the operation
after: Home the same day or next morning
Shoulder-tip pain from residual gas for a day or two
Normal diet resumed; some people notice looser stools after fatty meals
cholecystectomy.recovery: Most people return to normal activities within two weeks; heavy lifting avoided for a few weeks.
risks: Bile leak from the liver bed or cystic duct stump (1-2%)
Injury to the common bile duct (about 1 in 300), the serious complication
Bleeding, infection, retained stones in the duct
Conversion to open surgery (a few per cent, more in acute inflammation)
alternatives: Watchful waiting for stones with no symptoms
Antibiotics and a drainage tube (cholecystostomy) in patients too unwell for surgery
Bile-acid tablets for tiny stones (slow, often recur)

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

knee-replacement.name: Knee replacement
knee-replacement.what: The worn surfaces at the end of the femur and top of the tibia are cut away and capped with metal components, with a polyethylene insert between them as the new cartilage; the back of the kneecap is often resurfaced. A partial replacement treats one compartment only when the rest of the joint is healthy.
why: Severe osteoarthritis (or rheumatoid arthritis) with pain that limits walking, sleep and daily life despite painkillers, physiotherapy, weight loss and injections
Post-traumatic arthritis after fractures
Rarely, tumours or failed previous surgery
before: Standing X-rays; blood tests, ECG, MRSA screen, dental check
'Joint school' education, prehabilitation exercises, weight optimisation
Spinal or general anaesthetic with nerve blocks
steps: A vertical incision over the front of the knee; the kneecap is moved aside
Guided cuts remove a few millimetres from the end of the femur and top of the tibia, and worn cartilage and the cruciate ligaments as required
Trial components are fitted and the ligament balance and alignment checked through the full range of movement
The final metal components are cemented (or press-fitted) and the plastic insert locked in
The joint is washed, local anaesthetic infiltrated, and the layers closed
after: Standing and walking with a frame the same day or next
Physiotherapy from day one: bending, straightening, stairs; home in 1-3 days
Blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2-6 weeks; ice and elevation
Wound check at two weeks; six-week and one-year reviews
knee-replacement.recovery: Walking without aids by about six weeks, driving at 6-8 weeks, most of the benefit by three months and continued improvement for a year. A knee replacement usually lasts 15-25 years.
risks: Deep infection (about 1%), the most serious, sometimes needing revision
Blood clots in the leg or lung
Stiffness needing manipulation
Loosening or wear over time; a small number never feel quite right
Nerve or vessel injury, fracture around the implant (rare)
alternatives: Exercise programmes, weight loss, walking aids, bracing
Steroid or hyaluronic acid injections
Osteotomy (realigning the bone) in younger patients with one-sided wear
Arthroscopy is not helpful for degenerative knees

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

cataract-surgery.name: Cataract surgery
cataract-surgery.what: The cloudy natural lens of the eye is broken up with ultrasound through a 2-3 mm incision at the edge of the cornea and sucked out, and a folded plastic lens is injected into the empty lens capsule where it unfolds. Done under drops or a local anaesthetic injection in 15-30 minutes, it is the commonest operation in the world.
why: A cataract that blurs vision or causes glare enough to affect daily life, driving or work
Rarely, to see the retina for treating diabetic eye disease, or to lower eye pressure in glaucoma
before: Eye measurements (biometry) to choose the lens power, aiming for distance or near focus
Drops to dilate the pupil on the day; anaesthetic drops or a small injection
No need to fast for local anaesthetic; regular medicines continued
steps: A tiny self-sealing incision is made at the edge of the cornea
A circular opening is torn in the front of the lens capsule
An ultrasound probe emulsifies the lens nucleus, which is aspirated along with the softer cortex
The folded intraocular lens is injected into the capsule and unfolds into place
The incision seals without stitches; antibiotic is placed in the eye
after: Home within an hour with a clear shield to wear at night for a week
Antibiotic and anti-inflammatory drops for about four weeks
Vision usually clears within days; new glasses after 4-6 weeks
Avoid rubbing the eye, swimming and heavy lifting for a couple of weeks
cataract-surgery.recovery: Most people see well within a few days and resume driving within one to two weeks once the eye meets the standard. The second eye is done weeks later.
risks: Posterior capsule opacification (cloudy membrane behind the lens) in up to a fifth over years, cleared with a quick laser
Infection inside the eye (endophthalmitis, about 1 in 1000), sight-threatening
Tear of the capsule, retinal detachment, swelling of the retina, raised pressure
A refractive surprise needing glasses or a lens exchange
alternatives: Stronger glasses and better lighting while the cataract is mild
No surgery, if vision is acceptable; cataracts do not damage the eye by waiting except when very advanced

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

angioplasty.name: Coronary angioplasty and stenting
angioplasty.what: A narrowed or blocked coronary artery is opened from inside. A fine wire is steered across the narrowing through a catheter from the wrist or groin, a balloon is inflated to crush the plaque against the wall, and a drug-coated metal mesh stent is expanded to hold the artery open. As primary PCI it is the emergency treatment for a heart attack; electively it relieves angina.
why: ST-elevation heart attack (STEMI): open the artery within 120 minutes of diagnosis
Non-ST-elevation heart attack and unstable angina, usually within days
Stable angina not controlled by medication, or with a large area of ischaemia on testing
before: ECG, troponin, kidney function, clotting; a loading dose of aspirin and a second antiplatelet
Nil by mouth if elective; in an emergency straight to the catheter lab
Local anaesthetic to the wrist; mild sedation
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial (or femoral) artery and heparin given
Catheters are passed to the origin of each coronary artery and contrast injected to map the narrowings
A guidewire is steered across the lesion
A balloon is inflated for seconds to open the narrowing, with the ECG watched for ischaemia
A drug-eluting stent on a balloon is positioned and expanded to the artery's size; a final angiogram confirms flow
The sheath is removed and the wrist compressed with a band
after: Bed rest for a few hours (longer for femoral access); home the next day for elective cases, 2-3 days after a heart attack
Dual antiplatelet therapy for 6-12 months to stop clot forming on the stent, then aspirin for life
Statin, beta blocker and ACE inhibitor as indicated; cardiac rehabilitation
angioplasty.recovery: Back to light activity within days and work in a week or two for elective procedures; after a heart attack, structured rehabilitation over 6-12 weeks.
risks: Bruising or bleeding at the puncture site; rarely damage to the artery
Contrast kidney injury and allergy
Heart attack, stroke or death during the procedure (well under 1% electively, higher in emergencies)
Stent thrombosis (rare, but serious if antiplatelets are stopped early); restenosis within the stent over years
Emergency bypass surgery (rare)
alternatives: Medication alone for stable angina (equally good for survival in many cases)
Coronary artery bypass grafting for three-vessel or left main disease, especially with diabetes
Thrombolysis (clot-busting drugs) when PCI cannot be delivered in time

references.title: NHS: Coronary angioplasty and stent insertion
