amlodipine.name: Amlodipine
amlodipine.summary: A long-acting calcium channel blocker that relaxes artery walls to lower blood pressure and prevent angina, taken once daily and among the most prescribed medicines worldwide.
usedFor: High blood pressure (first choice over 55 and in people of Black African or Caribbean origin, or when an ACE inhibitor is not suitable)
Angina prevention
Non-dihydropyridine relatives (diltiazem, verapamil) also slow the heart and treat some fast rhythms
amlodipine.howItWorks: Blocks L-type calcium channels in the smooth muscle of artery walls. Muscle cells need calcium to contract, so with fewer channels open the arteries relax and widen, lowering resistance and blood pressure and letting more blood reach heart muscle. Amlodipine selects vessels over heart muscle, so it does not slow the heart; its long half-life gives smooth 24-hour control.
forms: Tablets 5 or 10 mg once daily
amlodipine.onset: Gradual, over days; steady state in about a week.

common: Ankle swelling (fluid leaking from widened capillaries, not heart failure; not helped by diuretics)
Flushing, headache, palpitations in the first weeks
Gum overgrowth, tiredness, dizziness
serious: Marked low blood pressure with fainting, particularly with other blood-pressure medicines or dehydration
Chest pain that is new or worse in the first days of treatment (rare reflex tachycardia)
Allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips or throat, difficulty breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (rare liver reaction)

cautions: Grapefruit juice increases levels of some calcium channel blockers
Severe aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, unstable angina
Simvastatin dose is limited with amlodipine
amlodipine.monitoring: Blood pressure; no blood tests needed for amlodipine.

references.title: NHS: Amlodipine
references.section: Taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements

routes: Oral (tablets, oral solution)
amlodipine.understand: Amlodipine relaxes the muscle in the walls of your arteries so that they widen. Blood flows through them with less resistance, which lowers blood pressure and lets more blood reach the heart muscle, which helps prevent angina.
amlodipine.mechanismDetail: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that binds the alpha-1 subunit of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle, preferring the inactivated channel state that predominates in depolarised arterial muscle. Reduced calcium influx lowers activation of myosin light-chain kinase, so arteriolar tone and total peripheral resistance fall while cardiac contractility and sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction are little affected at therapeutic doses (in contrast to verapamil and diltiazem). Coronary arteries and arterioles dilate, improving oxygen delivery in chronic stable and vasospastic angina. The slow onset and long elimination half-life (35-50 hours) give gradual, sustained 24-hour blood-pressure control without reflex tachycardia.

pathway.label: Reduced calcium entry into muscle cells

indications.note: Prophylaxis of chronic stable angina and vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina
Alone or with other medicines; also chronic stable and vasospastic angina and angiographically documented coronary artery disease

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

indications.note: NICE first-line choice for adults aged 55 or over and for adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin of any age, and the usual second agent added to an ACE inhibitor or ARB

warnings.text: Amlodipine may be prescribed with care, or a different medicine chosen, for people with severe heart failure, because dihydropyridines can worsen fluid retention in some patients; the BNF lists heart failure among its cautions.
Dizziness, particularly when standing up, is common in the first weeks; UK information advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery if affected.
Amlodipine is cleared by the liver; in hepatic impairment the half-life is prolonged and a lower starting dose is advised, with slow titration in severe impairment.

Ankle swelling is a dose-related effect of dihydropyridines caused by widened capillaries, not by heart failure, and does not respond to diuretics; it is a reason to review the dose rather than to add a water tablet.

contraindications.text: Amlodipine is contraindicated in cardiogenic shock.
Contraindicated in unstable angina; amlodipine is for stable and vasospastic angina.
Contraindicated in significant aortic stenosis, where vasodilation can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure.
Previous allergic reaction to amlodipine or another dihydropyridine.

hepatic.text: Half-life is prolonged in liver disease; start with a low dose and increase slowly, particularly in severe hepatic impairment.

In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction amlodipine is neutral for survival but may worsen oedema; it is used with care when blood pressure control is needed.

furosemide.name: Furosemide
furosemide.summary: A powerful loop diuretic that makes the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour, used to clear fluid overload in heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease.
usedFor: Fluid overload in heart failure: breathlessness, swollen legs, fluid on the lungs (intravenous in emergencies)
Oedema from kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome) and liver cirrhosis (with spironolactone)
High blood pressure when kidney function is poor
Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide) are the gentler relatives used for blood pressure
furosemide.howItWorks: Blocks the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the segment that reabsorbs a quarter of all filtered sodium. Salt that stays in the tubule drags water with it, so urine output can rise several-fold within an hour. Potassium, magnesium and calcium are lost too, and the kidney compensates by activating the renin-angiotensin system.
forms: Tablets 20, 40, 500 mg; oral solution; intravenous injection or infusion
furosemide.onset: Oral within an hour, lasting about 6 hours (hence the name Lasix: 'lasts six'); intravenous within minutes.

common: Passing lots of urine, urgency (take in the morning)
Dizziness on standing, dehydration, thirst, cramps
Low potassium, sodium and magnesium; raised uric acid (gout) and glucose
serious: Acute kidney injury from over-diuresis
Dangerous potassium or sodium disturbance and arrhythmia
Hearing loss (ototoxicity) with rapid high intravenous doses, especially with aminoglycosides
Collapse from low blood pressure in the frail

cautions: Daily weights in heart failure guide the dose: a gain of 2 kg in 3 days often means more diuretic
Pause on sick days with vomiting or diarrhoea
Care with lithium, digoxin, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides
Severe low potassium or sodium, anuria, dehydration: do not use until corrected
furosemide.monitoring: Kidney function and electrolytes within a week of starting or changing dose, then regularly; weight and blood pressure.

glyceryl-trinitrate.name: Glyceryl trinitrate
glyceryl-trinitrate.summary: A fast-acting nitrate spray or tablet under the tongue that widens veins and coronary arteries to relieve an angina attack within minutes.
usedFor: Relieving an angina attack within minutes (spray or tablet under the tongue)
Preventing angina before exertion
Intravenous infusion for unstable angina, heart attack with ongoing pain and acute heart failure
Long-acting isosorbide mononitrate for regular angina prevention; GTN ointment for anal fissures
glyceryl-trinitrate.howItWorks: Releases nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle, activating guanylate cyclase and relaxing the vessel. Veins dilate most, so less blood returns to the heart and it has less to pump against (lower preload and wall tension, lower oxygen demand); coronary arteries and collaterals widen, improving supply to ischaemic muscle. Relief within one to three minutes helps confirm that chest pain was angina, though oesophageal spasm responds too.
forms: Sublingual spray 400 micrograms per dose or tablets; patches; intravenous infusion; modified-release tablets (isosorbide)

common: Throbbing headache (from dilated scalp vessels), flushing
Dizziness and faintness from a drop in blood pressure: sit down before using
serious: Severe hypotension and collapse if combined with sildenafil or similar drugs (contraindicated within 24-48 hours)
Fast heart rate; rarely worsening of angina; methaemoglobinaemia with prolonged infusion

cautions: Tolerance develops with continuous exposure: long-acting nitrates need a nitrate-free interval each day
If pain persists 5 minutes after a second dose, call emergency services: it may be a heart attack
Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, very low blood pressure, raised intracranial pressure
Tablets lose potency after 8 weeks once opened; sprays last longer
glyceryl-trinitrate.monitoring: Blood pressure during infusions; frequency of spray use is a marker of angina control.

regulatory.note: Sublingual spray and tablets are pharmacy (P) medicines
Patches, buccal tablets and infusions

apixaban.name: Apixaban and DOACs
apixaban.summary: A direct oral anticoagulant that blocks clotting factor Xa, preventing strokes in atrial fibrillation and treating deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism without routine blood monitoring.
usedFor: Preventing stroke in atrial fibrillation (first choice over warfarin for most)
Treating and preventing deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Preventing clots after hip and knee replacement
Not used for mechanical heart valves or antiphospholipid syndrome (warfarin remains)
apixaban.howItWorks: Binds directly to activated factor X, the enzyme at the junction of the clotting cascade that converts prothrombin to thrombin. Less thrombin means less fibrin, so clots that form in the slow-flowing left atrial appendage or leg veins are prevented or stopped from growing. Unlike warfarin the effect is predictable, starts within hours, needs no blood-level monitoring and is little affected by diet.
forms: Tablets 2.5 or 5 mg twice daily (rivaroxaban and edoxaban once daily)
apixaban.onset: Peak effect 3-4 hours after a dose; wears off within a day or two of stopping.

common: Bruising, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavier periods
Nausea, anaemia
serious: Major bleeding: gastrointestinal, intracranial (about half the rate of warfarin), retroperitoneal
Bleeding after trauma or surgery; reversal agents (andexanet, idarucizumab for dabigatran) exist but are limited
Spinal haematoma with epidural anaesthesia

cautions: Dose reduced with kidney impairment, low weight, age over 80 (apixaban), and some interacting drugs
Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless specifically advised; alcohol in moderation
Stop 24-72 hours before surgery depending on bleeding risk and kidney function
Missed doses matter because the effect wears off quickly; do not double up
apixaban.monitoring: Kidney function, blood count and weight at least yearly (more often if kidney function is poor); no INR needed.

warfarin.name: Warfarin
warfarin.summary: The long-established oral anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors; effective for mechanical heart valves and clots but needs regular INR blood tests and careful dosing.
usedFor: Mechanical heart valves (the only oral anticoagulant licensed)
Atrial fibrillation with moderate or severe mitral stenosis, and antiphospholipid syndrome
Venous thromboembolism where DOACs are unsuitable (severe kidney failure, cost)
Historically the standard anticoagulant, now largely replaced by DOACs for other indications
warfarin.howItWorks: Blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver, so vitamin K cannot be recycled to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Existing factors take days to be cleared, so the effect starts after 2-3 days and heparin cover is needed for immediate protection. The dose needed varies enormously between people and with diet, illness and other drugs, so the INR blood test tunes it.
forms: Tablets 0.5, 1, 3 and 5 mg (colour-coded), taken once daily at the same time
warfarin.onset: Therapeutic after 3-5 days; effect persists 3-5 days after stopping. Reversed with vitamin K (slow) or prothrombin complex concentrate (immediate).

common: Bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds
Hair thinning, rash
serious: Major bleeding, including intracranial: risk rises steeply when the INR is above 4
Skin necrosis in the first days (protein C deficiency), purple toe syndrome
Fetal harm: teratogenic in the first trimester and bleeding later

cautions: Hundreds of interactions: antibiotics, antifungals, amiodarone, NSAIDs, alcohol binges raise the INR; rifampicin, carbamazepine, large amounts of green vegetables lower it
Keep vitamin K intake steady rather than avoiding it
Carry an anticoagulant alert card; tell dentists and pharmacists
Target INR 2-3 for most indications, 2.5-3.5 for some mechanical valves
warfarin.monitoring: INR every few days at first, then every 4-12 weeks once stable, and after any new drug or illness; self-testing meters are available.

metformin.name: Metformin
metformin.summary: The first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it reduces the glucose the liver releases and improves the body's response to insulin, without causing low blood sugar on its own.
usedFor: First-line drug for type 2 diabetes alongside diet and exercise
Prediabetes in people at high risk
Polycystic ovary syndrome (off label) and gestational diabetes
metformin.howItWorks: Reduces the amount of glucose the liver releases into blood (by inhibiting gluconeogenesis via AMP-activated protein kinase and the mitochondrial redox state), increases the sensitivity of muscle and fat to insulin, and modestly reduces glucose absorption from the gut. It does not stimulate insulin release, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own or weight gain; HbA1c falls by about 11 mmol/mol (1%).
forms: Tablets 500 mg and 850 mg with meals, up to 2 g daily; modified-release once daily for those with gut side effects; oral solution
metformin.onset: Glucose lowering within days; full effect in 2-3 weeks. Started low and increased weekly.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, bloating, metallic taste (a third at the start, most settle; take with food, build up slowly, or use modified release)
Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use
serious: Lactic acidosis: very rare, but dangerous when the drug accumulates in kidney failure, or in severe illness, dehydration, sepsis, heart failure or heavy alcohol use
Hypoglycaemia only when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas

cautions: Dose reduced when eGFR is below 45 and stopped below 30
Pause during acute illness with dehydration ('sick day rules') and around iodine contrast scans and surgery
Check B12 if anaemia, tingling or fatigue develop
Alcohol in moderation
metformin.monitoring: HbA1c every 3-6 months; kidney function at least yearly; B12 periodically.

routes: Oral (immediate-release and modified-release tablets, oral solution, powder sachets)
metformin.understand: Metformin lowers blood glucose mainly by telling the liver to release less sugar between meals, and by helping muscle respond to insulin. It does not make the pancreas release more insulin, so on its own it does not cause low blood sugar.
metformin.mechanismDetail: Metformin accumulates in hepatocytes via the OCT1 transporter and reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis: it lowers the mitochondrial energy state (partial inhibition of complex I and of mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase, shifting the cytosolic redox state) and activates AMP-activated protein kinase, which suppresses gluconeogenic gene expression and lipogenesis. Peripheral insulin sensitivity improves modestly, intestinal glucose uptake and GLP-1 secretion increase, and the gut microbiome changes. Because insulin secretion is not stimulated, hypoglycaemia does not occur with monotherapy and weight is neutral or slightly reduced. Metformin is not metabolised and is cleared by the kidney (tubular secretion); accumulation in renal failure, hypoxia or severe illness impairs lactate clearance and can precipitate lactic acidosis. It reduces ileal vitamin B12 absorption.

Iodinated contrast media: metformin is withheld on the day of a contrast procedure and for 48 hours afterwards in people with reduced kidney function, and restarted once kidney function is confirmed stable.

insulin.name: Insulin
insulin.summary: The hormone that moves glucose from the blood into cells, given by injection or pump to everyone with type 1 diabetes and to many with type 2 when other treatments are not enough.
usedFor: Type 1 diabetes: essential for life from diagnosis
Type 2 diabetes when tablets no longer control glucose, in pregnancy, and during severe illness or surgery
Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar states (intravenous infusion)
Lowering dangerously high potassium (with glucose) in emergencies
insulin.howItWorks: Replaces the hormone the pancreatic beta cells no longer make. Insulin binds receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells, moving GLUT4 transporters to the surface so glucose enters cells; it switches the liver from making glucose to storing glycogen, stops fat breakdown and ketone production, and promotes protein synthesis. Modern analogue insulins are engineered to act fast at meals (aspart, lispro) or flat and long as background (glargine, degludec), mimicking the natural pattern of a basal trickle plus mealtime bursts.
forms: Prefilled pens injected under the skin of the abdomen, thighs or buttocks, rotating sites; insulin pumps delivering rapid-acting insulin continuously; intravenous infusion in hospital; hybrid closed-loop systems with continuous glucose monitors
insulin.onset: Rapid-acting 10-20 minutes (peak 1-3 hours, lasts 3-5 hours); long-acting flat over 24 hours or more.

common: Hypoglycaemia (shaking, sweating, hunger, confusion): treat with 15-20 g fast sugar, recheck, then a snack
Weight gain
Lipohypertrophy (fatty lumps) at over-used injection sites, which absorb insulin erratically
Bruising, stinging
serious: Severe hypoglycaemia with seizure or coma, needing glucagon injection or intravenous glucose
Diabetic ketoacidosis if insulin is omitted in type 1 diabetes (never stop, even when not eating: adjust instead)
Hypokalaemia with intravenous infusion
Allergy (very rare with modern insulins)

cautions: Doses are individual and adjusted for food, activity, illness and glucose readings; errors in units are a major cause of harm ('units' written in full)
Sick-day rules: keep taking basal insulin, check glucose and ketones more often, drink fluids
Driving rules: check glucose before and every 2 hours; carry fast sugar
Store unopened insulin in the fridge; in use at room temperature for 4 weeks
insulin.monitoring: Fingerprick or continuous glucose monitoring several times daily; HbA1c every 3-6 months; annual eye, foot and kidney checks.

levothyroxine.name: Levothyroxine
levothyroxine.summary: Synthetic thyroid hormone (T4) that replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring energy, weight and metabolism; the dose is set by regular TSH blood tests.
usedFor: Hypothyroidism from any cause (autoimmune, after surgery or radioiodine, congenital)

levothyroxine.howItWorks: A synthetic copy of thyroxine (T4), the hormone the thyroid normally releases. Tissues convert it to the active T3, which enters cell nuclei and switches on genes controlling metabolic rate, heat production, heart rate, gut motility, growth and brain development. Replacement restores the pituitary's TSH to normal, which is how the dose is tuned.
forms: Tablets 25, 50, 100 micrograms and oral solution, once daily on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast (or at bedtime)
levothyroxine.onset: Symptoms improve over weeks; TSH takes 6-8 weeks to settle after each dose change. Lifelong.

serious: Angina or atrial fibrillation if started too fast in the elderly or those with heart disease (start at 25 micrograms)
Bone loss and atrial fibrillation with long-term over-replacement
Adrenal crisis if given before untreated adrenal insufficiency is corrected

cautions: Absorption falls with calcium, iron, antacids, proton pump inhibitors, soya and coffee: separate by 4 hours
Dose often needs to rise in pregnancy (increase by 25-50% and check TSH promptly), and with oestrogen, enzyme inducers
Stay on the same brand where possible
Do not use for weight loss in people with normal thyroid function

salbutamol.name: Salbutamol
salbutamol.summary: The blue reliever inhaler: a short-acting beta-2 agonist that opens the airways within minutes to relieve asthma and COPD symptoms during an attack or before exercise.
usedFor: Relief of wheeze and breathlessness in asthma and COPD ('reliever')
Before exercise in exercise-induced asthma
Nebulised or intravenous in severe asthma attacks and COPD flares

salbutamol.howItWorks: Stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors on the smooth muscle wrapped around the bronchi. This raises cyclic AMP inside the muscle cells, relaxing them within minutes so the airways widen and air moves more freely. It relieves the narrowing but does nothing for the underlying inflammation, which is why needing it more than twice a week signals poorly controlled asthma and the need for a preventer.
forms: Pressurised metered-dose inhaler 100 micrograms per puff (best with a spacer), dry powder inhaler, nebuliser solution, tablets and syrup (rarely), intravenous
salbutamol.onset: Within 5 minutes, peak 15-30 minutes, lasts 4-6 hours.

common: Fine tremor, fast heartbeat, palpitations, headache
Feeling shaky or restless; muscle cramps
serious: Low potassium with high doses (with steroids, diuretics, theophylline)
Arrhythmias in people with heart disease at high doses
Paradoxical bronchospasm (rare); over-reliance masking worsening asthma, linked to asthma deaths

cautions: Using more than three canisters a year, or needing it daily, means the asthma plan needs review
Anti-inflammatory reliever (budesonide-formoterol) is now preferred as the sole reliever in many guidelines

Beta blockers antagonise the effect

inhaled-corticosteroids.name: Inhaled corticosteroids
inhaled-corticosteroids.summary: The preventer inhalers of asthma: low doses of steroid delivered straight into the airways damp down inflammation so attacks become rarer and milder.
inhaled-corticosteroids.class: Inhaled glucocorticoid (with or without a long-acting beta-2 agonist)
usedFor: The cornerstone of asthma treatment: daily to prevent attacks and control symptoms
COPD with frequent exacerbations and high blood eosinophils, combined with long-acting bronchodilators

inhaled-corticosteroids.howItWorks: Steroid molecules deposited on the airway lining diffuse into cells and bind glucocorticoid receptors, which move to the nucleus and switch off the genes for inflammatory cytokines, reduce eosinophils and mast cells, and shrink mucosal swelling and mucus. Inhaling delivers a tiny dose straight to the airways, so the whole-body effects of steroid tablets are largely avoided. Benefit builds over days to weeks and depends on daily use.

At high doses long term: adrenal suppression, reduced bone density, cataract and glaucoma, easy bruising, a small effect on growth in children
Sudden stopping of high doses can unmask adrenal insufficiency

cautions: Use the lowest dose that keeps control, stepped up or down at review
Long-acting beta agonists must never be used alone in asthma without a steroid
Carry a steroid card at high doses; check bone density if on high dose for years

omeprazole.name: Omeprazole
omeprazole.summary: A proton pump inhibitor that switches off acid production in the stomach, healing ulcers and reflux oesophagitis and protecting the stomach from anti-inflammatory drugs.
usedFor: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and its complications (oesophagitis, Barrett oesophagus)

omeprazole.howItWorks: Irreversibly blocks the hydrogen-potassium ATPase, the 'proton pump' in the parietal cells of the stomach lining that secretes acid as the final step of every stimulus. Because the pump is disabled rather than the signals, acid falls by over 90%, and new pumps must be made before secretion recovers, so the effect outlasts the drug's short half-life. Given 30-60 minutes before breakfast, when pumps are most active.
forms: Capsules and tablets 10, 20, 40 mg once or twice daily; oral suspension; intravenous

common: Headache, nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain

serious: Low magnesium with long-term use (cramps, arrhythmia)
Clostridioides difficile and other gut infections, and pneumonia (acid normally kills swallowed microbes)
Reduced absorption of B12, iron and calcium; a modest increase in fractures with prolonged high-dose use
Acute interstitial nephritis and, rarely, subacute cutaneous lupus

cautions: Use the lowest effective dose and review long-term use; rebound acid hypersecretion for a few weeks after stopping
May mask stomach cancer symptoms: alarm features (weight loss, swallowing difficulty, bleeding, age over 55 with new symptoms) need endoscopy first
Omeprazole reduces the activation of clopidogrel (pantoprazole preferred); stop two weeks before H. pylori testing
Interactions with methotrexate, some HIV drugs

routes: Oral (gastro-resistant capsules and tablets, oral suspension); intravenous
omeprazole.understand: Omeprazole switches off the acid pumps in the cells of your stomach lining, so far less acid is made. With less acid, ulcers can heal, the oesophagus is no longer burned by reflux, and the stomach is protected from anti-inflammatory painkillers.
omeprazole.mechanismDetail: Omeprazole is a substituted benzimidazole prodrug. Absorbed from gastro-resistant granules, it concentrates in the acidic secretory canaliculi of gastric parietal cells, where it is protonated and converted to a sulfenamide that forms covalent disulphide bonds with cysteines on the H+/K+ ATPase, inhibiting the pump irreversibly. Because the pump is the final step of acid secretion, basal and stimulated acid output fall by more than 90%; secretion recovers only as new pumps are synthesised (half-life of pump turnover about 50 hours), so once-daily dosing before breakfast gives a sustained effect despite a plasma half-life of about an hour. Omeprazole is metabolised by CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 and inhibits CYP2C19, reducing activation of clopidogrel and raising levels of some other drugs. Long-term acid suppression raises gastrin, alters absorption of magnesium, calcium, iron and vitamin B12, and changes the gut microbiome.

Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus: a rare skin reaction to PPIs, presenting as a rash in sun-exposed skin with joint pain; the drug is stopped.

amoxicillin.name: Amoxicillin
amoxicillin.summary: A widely used penicillin antibiotic that kills bacteria by breaking their cell walls, prescribed for chest, ear, sinus, dental and some urinary infections and as part of Helicobacter pylori treatment; useless against viruses and dangerous only in true penicillin allergy.
usedFor: Chest infections and community-acquired pneumonia
Ear, sinus and throat infections caused by bacteria
Dental infections; H. pylori eradication (with a PPI and clarithromycin)
Urinary infections use nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; skin infections flucloxacillin; atypical pneumonia doxycycline or clarithromycin
amoxicillin.howItWorks: Binds the penicillin-binding proteins that bacteria use to cross-link the peptidoglycan of their cell wall. Growing bacteria with a weakened wall burst under their own osmotic pressure. Human cells have no cell wall, which is why penicillins are so selective. Bacteria fight back with beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug; clavulanic acid (in co-amoxiclav) blocks that enzyme. Antibiotics do nothing against viruses, the cause of most sore throats, colds and coughs.
forms: Capsules 250 and 500 mg, oral suspension, sachets; intravenous injection; usually three times daily for 5 days
amoxicillin.onset: Improvement within 48-72 hours; the full course is decided by the infection, not by symptoms.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, thrush
Non-allergic rash (very common in glandular fever, where amoxicillin should be avoided)
serious: Anaphylaxis in true penicillin allergy (about 1 in 10,000 courses); most reported 'penicillin allergies' are not true allergy and can be safely delabelled
Clostridioides difficile colitis, especially with broad-spectrum agents in hospital
Liver injury with co-amoxiclav (cholestatic hepatitis), seizures at very high doses in kidney failure
Antimicrobial resistance across the population with every unnecessary course

cautions: Take the course as prescribed; do not save leftovers or share
Report any previous reaction so an alternative (clarithromycin, doxycycline) can be chosen
Doxycycline: sun sensitivity, not for pregnancy or young children; nitrofurantoin: avoid with poor kidney function
Warfarin levels may rise with many antibiotics
amoxicillin.monitoring: Clinical response at 48-72 hours; cultures before starting where possible so therapy can be narrowed.

routes: Oral (capsules, oral suspension, sachets); intravenous and intramuscular injection
amoxicillin.understand: Amoxicillin attacks the wall that holds a bacterium together. Growing bacteria with a damaged wall burst and die. Human cells have no such wall, so the drug leaves them alone, but it also cannot touch viruses, which have no wall either.
amoxicillin.mechanismDetail: Amoxicillin is an aminopenicillin, a beta-lactam that binds and inactivates penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) in the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, preventing cross-linking of peptidoglycan during cell-wall synthesis; autolytic enzymes then lyse the growing cell, so the effect is bactericidal and time-dependent (efficacy depends on the time the concentration stays above the MIC, hence three-times-daily dosing). Its spectrum covers streptococci including most pneumococci, many enterococci, Listeria, Haemophilus (non-beta-lactamase producers), Helicobacter pylori and some Enterobacterales, but it is destroyed by beta-lactamases; clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav inhibits many of them. Amoxicillin is better absorbed orally than ampicillin and is excreted largely unchanged by the kidney, so doses are reduced in severe renal impairment and levels are raised by probenecid.

pathway.label: Infection cleared in the lungs, ears, sinuses, teeth, urinary tract
Pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis, H. pylori

indications.note: Community-acquired pneumonia; also acute exacerbations of COPD, bronchitis

indications.text: Acute otitis media, acute sinusitis, streptococcal tonsillitis, dental abscess, Lyme disease, Listeria meningitis (intravenous), endocarditis prophylaxis in some circumstances

indications.note: Helicobacter pylori eradication with a proton pump inhibitor and a second antibiotic
Lower urinary tract infection only when the organism is known to be susceptible; resistance is common
Infections of the ears, nose, throat, urinary tract and skin caused by susceptible bacteria; with other medicines for H. pylori
NICE: first-choice oral antibiotic for community-acquired pneumonia of low and moderate severity (with a macrolide added for moderate severity)

indications.note: NICE: a first-choice antibiotic for an acute exacerbation of COPD when an antibiotic is indicated

source.title: NICE NG109: Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing

indications.note: NICE: amoxicillin only if culture results confirm susceptibility; nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim are first choice

warnings.text: Allergy: anaphylaxis occurs in a small minority of people with true penicillin allergy; UK information advises stopping and seeking emergency help for swelling of the face, lips or throat, wheeze, tight chest or a widespread itchy rash. A previous serious reaction to any penicillin is a contraindication.

Rash in glandular fever: a widespread non-allergic rash is very common when amoxicillin is given during infectious mononucleosis (and with some leukaemias), so it is avoided when glandular fever is suspected.
Antibiotic-associated colitis: severe or persistent diarrhoea during or after treatment may be Clostridioides difficile infection, particularly in hospital and in older people.

Doses are reduced in severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 for high doses, below 10 for standard doses) because amoxicillin is excreted by the kidney; crystalluria can occur with high doses and poor hydration.
Antimicrobial resistance: every unnecessary course selects resistant bacteria; the drug does not treat viral sore throats, colds or most coughs, and the course is completed as prescribed.

contraindications.text: Contraindicated in people with a history of hypersensitivity to penicillins; those with a history of immediate hypersensitivity to any beta-lactam should not receive it.
Avoided because of the high rate of rash; not a true allergy but a reason to choose another antibiotic.

monitoringPlan.why: Improvement expected within 48-72 hours; if not, the diagnosis, the organism and the antibiotic are reviewed
Sputum, urine or blood cultures so that treatment can be narrowed to the organism

monitoringPlan.what: Kidney function in high-dose or prolonged treatment
monitoringPlan.why: To adjust the dose in renal impairment

pregnancy.text: UK information states amoxicillin is safe to take during pregnancy; it is one of the antibiotics most often used.

lactation.text: UK information states amoxicillin can be taken while breastfeeding; small amounts pass into milk and may occasionally cause loose stools or thrush in the baby.

children.text: Licensed from birth at weight- or age-based doses; the liquid form is used for children and a rash in a child with a viral illness should be assessed rather than assumed to be allergy.

older.text: No dose change unless kidney function is reduced; higher risk of C. difficile colitis.

renal.text: Reduce the dose or frequency when eGFR is below 30 for high-dose regimens and below 10 for standard doses; maintain hydration at high doses to avoid crystalluria.

hepatic.text: No dose adjustment for amoxicillin itself; co-amoxiclav (with clavulanic acid) can cause cholestatic jaundice, more often in older people and with longer courses.

foodInteractions.effect: Absorption is not significantly affected by food; amoxicillin can be taken before or after meals, spaced evenly through the day.
foodInteractions.management: UK information states amoxicillin can be taken with or without food.

Chronic kidney disease: dose and frequency reduced in severe impairment.
Urinary tract infection: resistance is common, so amoxicillin is used only when culture confirms susceptibility.

Amoxicillin can cause a false-positive urine glucose result with copper-reduction tests (not with enzyme-based dipsticks).

Warfarin: amoxicillin can raise the INR in some people by altering gut flora and vitamin K; extra INR checks are advised.

cetirizine.name: Cetirizine and antihistamines
cetirizine.summary: A non-drowsy second-generation antihistamine that blocks histamine H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and other allergic symptoms.
usedFor: Hay fever and year-round allergic rhinitis: sneezing, runny nose, itchy eyes
Urticaria (hives) and itching
Mild allergic reactions to foods, insect bites and drugs (not a substitute for adrenaline in anaphylaxis)
Sedating first-generation antihistamines (chlorphenamine, promethazine) for short-term itch or nausea
cetirizine.howItWorks: Blocks H1 histamine receptors on blood vessels, nerves and smooth muscle. When mast cells release histamine in response to an allergen, it normally makes capillaries leak (swelling, runny nose), stimulates itch nerves and constricts airways; with the receptors occupied, those effects are muted. Second-generation drugs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so they cause much less drowsiness than older ones.
forms: Tablets 10 mg once daily, oral solution for children, eye drops and nasal sprays of related agents

common: Mild drowsiness (about 1 in 10, more than loratadine or fexofenadine), dry mouth, headache, tiredness
serious: Marked sedation and impaired driving with first-generation agents; confusion and falls in the elderly, urinary retention in men with prostate enlargement
QT prolongation with some older non-sedating agents (withdrawn); rare hypersensitivity

cautions: Check driving response with any antihistamine; avoid alcohol
Dose reduced in kidney impairment for cetirizine
Not for children under 2 without advice; sedating antihistamines avoided in young children
Anaphylaxis needs adrenaline first: antihistamines are adjuncts only

sertraline.name: Sertraline and SSRIs
sertraline.summary: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant used for depression, anxiety disorders, panic and obsessive-compulsive disorder; it takes several weeks to work fully.
usedFor: Moderate to severe depression, alongside psychological therapy
Anxiety disorders: generalised anxiety, panic disorder, social anxiety, PTSD, OCD
Sertraline is a first choice after a heart attack because of its cardiac safety
sertraline.howItWorks: Blocks the serotonin transporter that pumps serotonin back into the nerve ending after release, so more remains in the synapse. The immediate rise in serotonin is not itself the cure: over weeks, receptors adapt, and growth factors such as BDNF and neuroplasticity in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex increase, which is thought to underlie the delayed improvement in mood and anxiety.
forms: Tablets 25-200 mg once daily, morning or evening
sertraline.onset: Side effects first; mood benefit begins at 2-4 weeks, full at 6-8 weeks. Continued for at least 6 months after recovery.

common: Nausea, diarrhoea, headache, sweating, insomnia or drowsiness in the first weeks
Sexual dysfunction (reduced libido, delayed orgasm), which often persists
Increased anxiety and agitation at the start
serious: Increased suicidal thoughts in the first weeks, particularly under 25: close follow-up
Bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants (serotonin is needed for platelet function)
Low sodium in the elderly; serotonin syndrome with tramadol, triptans, MAOIs, St John's wort
Discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, electric-shock sensations, irritability) if stopped abruptly: taper over weeks

cautions: Review within 1-2 weeks of starting, sooner in young people
Do not stop suddenly
Citalopram and escitalopram prolong the QT interval: dose limits and ECG in heart disease
Pregnancy: discuss risks and benefits; sertraline is among the better studied
sertraline.monitoring: Mood and suicidality at review; sodium in the elderly; ECG for citalopram at high doses.

prednisolone.name: Prednisolone and steroids
prednisolone.summary: A corticosteroid tablet that suppresses inflammation and the immune system, used in asthma flare-ups, arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and many autoimmune conditions.
usedFor: Asthma attacks and COPD flares (5-day courses)
Flares of rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, gout, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis
Autoimmune disease, severe allergic reactions, some cancers and transplant rejection
Replacing cortisol in adrenal insufficiency (hydrocortisone); dexamethasone in brain swelling and severe COVID-19
prednisolone.howItWorks: A synthetic version of cortisol, the adrenal stress hormone, at doses far above what the body makes. It enters cells and binds glucocorticoid receptors that switch off genes for inflammatory cytokines and switch on anti-inflammatory ones, shrinking the whole inflammatory response, whatever its trigger: it does not treat the cause. The same receptors in liver, muscle, bone, skin and brain produce the side effects, and prolonged dosing suppresses the pituitary-adrenal axis so the body's own cortisol production shuts down.
forms: Tablets 1, 5, 25 mg taken once in the morning with food; soluble tablets; intravenous hydrocortisone and methylprednisolone; joint injections; creams, inhalers, eye drops for local use
prednisolone.onset: Anti-inflammatory effect within hours; symptom relief in asthma and arthritis within a day or two.

common: Increased appetite and weight gain, fluid retention, mood change, insomnia
Raised blood glucose (new or worsened diabetes), raised blood pressure
Indigestion; thin skin, bruising, acne
serious: Adrenal suppression: after more than 3 weeks the dose must be tapered, and extra cover is needed for illness and surgery; abrupt stopping can cause an adrenal crisis
Osteoporosis and fractures (bone protection with bisphosphonates for long courses), avascular necrosis of the hip
Infections (masked and more severe: chickenpox, shingles, TB reactivation), peptic ulcer with NSAIDs, cataract and glaucoma
Psychosis, severe mood disturbance; growth suppression in children; muscle wasting

cautions: Carry a steroid emergency card on courses longer than 3-4 weeks
Never stop long-term steroids suddenly; sick-day doubling rules
Check for TB, hepatitis, diabetes and blood pressure before long courses; consider PPI and bone protection
Live vaccines avoided on high doses; report exposure to chickenpox if not immune
prednisolone.monitoring: Blood pressure, glucose, weight; bone density and eye checks on long courses.

allopurinol.name: Allopurinol
allopurinol.summary: A xanthine oxidase inhibitor that lowers uric acid in the blood, taken every day to prevent gout attacks and kidney stones rather than to treat an acute attack.
usedFor: Preventing gout attacks by lowering blood uric acid (started after the first attack settles, especially with repeated attacks, tophi, kidney stones or kidney disease)
Preventing uric acid kidney stones
Preventing tumour lysis syndrome during chemotherapy
allopurinol.howItWorks: Blocks xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid at the end of purine breakdown. Blood urate falls below its saturation point, so no new crystals form and existing deposits in joints and tophi slowly dissolve over months. The dose is increased every few weeks until the urate target (below 360, or 300 micromol/L with tophi) is reached.
forms: Tablets 100 and 300 mg once daily after food, starting at 100 mg (50 mg in kidney disease) and titrating up to 900 mg
allopurinol.onset: Urate falls within days, but attacks can increase for the first 3-6 months as crystals dissolve, so colchicine or an NSAID is given as cover.

common: Rash (stop if it appears), nausea, diarrhoea
Gout flares in the first months
serious: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome: severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson, toxic epidermal necrolysis) with liver and kidney involvement, rare but life-threatening, more likely in those with the HLA-B*58:01 gene (common in Han Chinese, Thai and Korean populations, who are screened), kidney disease and high starting doses
Bone marrow suppression, liver injury (rare)

cautions: Do not start during an acute attack; do not stop during an attack once established
Interactions: azathioprine and mercaptopurine (levels rise dangerously), warfarin, ACE inhibitors and thiazides (hypersensitivity risk)
Drink plenty of fluid; reduce dose in kidney impairment
Febuxostat is the alternative if allopurinol is not tolerated, with cardiovascular caution
allopurinol.monitoring: Serum urate every 4 weeks during titration, then yearly; kidney and liver function.

alendronate.name: Alendronate
alendronate.summary: A weekly bisphosphonate that slows bone breakdown, strengthening bone in osteoporosis and cutting the risk of hip and spine fractures.
usedFor: Osteoporosis: preventing hip, spine and wrist fractures in postmenopausal women and men at high risk
Bone protection during long courses of steroid tablets
Zoledronic acid infusions for osteoporosis (yearly), Paget disease, bone metastases and high calcium in cancer
alendronate.howItWorks: The drug binds tightly to bone mineral, and when osteoclasts (the cells that dissolve bone) resorb that surface they take it up, which disables their metabolism and triggers their death. Resorption falls while bone-building osteoblasts keep working for a time, so bone density rises by a few per cent and, more importantly, the microarchitecture is preserved; hip fractures fall by about 40% and spine fractures by half.
forms: Tablets 70 mg once weekly (or 10 mg daily), swallowed with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, standing or sitting upright for 30 minutes before food, drink or other medicines; effervescent and liquid forms; risedronate weekly; ibandronate monthly; zoledronic acid infusion yearly
alendronate.onset: Bone turnover falls within weeks; fracture reduction from about a year. Usually 5 years, then reviewed (drug 'holiday').

common: Indigestion, heartburn, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhoea
Muscle and joint aches; flu-like illness after the first zoledronic acid infusion
serious: Oesophageal ulcers and strictures if the dosing instructions are not followed
Osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare, mostly with high-dose cancer regimens; dental check before starting)
Atypical femoral fractures after many years of use (thigh pain is a warning)
Low calcium, eye inflammation, kidney impairment with intravenous forms

cautions: Correct vitamin D deficiency and ensure adequate calcium before starting
Not used with eGFR below 35, swallowing disorders, active oesophageal disease, or inability to sit upright
Dental review and good oral hygiene; tell the dentist
Review at 5 years (3 for zoledronate): continue in those at highest risk
alendronate.monitoring: Bone density scan every 3-5 years; calcium and vitamin D; kidney function for intravenous forms.

losartan.name: Losartan
losartan.summary: An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) that relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure and protect the kidneys in diabetes, an alternative for people who cough on ACE inhibitors.
usedFor: High blood pressure, particularly when an ACE inhibitor causes cough
Protecting the kidneys in type 2 diabetes with protein in the urine
Heart failure (candesartan, valsartan and losartan are the ARBs used) when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated
Reducing stroke risk in hypertension with a thickened left ventricle
losartan.howItWorks: Blocks the AT1 receptor that angiotensin II uses to constrict arteries, release aldosterone from the adrenal glands and thicken heart and vessel walls. With the receptor occupied, arteries relax, pressure falls, and the heart and the kidney's filters are unloaded. Because the converting enzyme is untouched, bradykinin does not build up, so the dry cough of ACE inhibitors is rare.
forms: Tablets 25, 50 and 100 mg once daily
losartan.onset: Blood pressure falls over the first week; full effect in 3-6 weeks.

common: Dizziness, especially on standing at first
Tiredness, headache
A small rise in potassium and creatinine
serious: Acute kidney injury when dehydrated, with NSAIDs, or with narrowed renal arteries
High potassium with potassium supplements, spironolactone or kidney disease
Angio-oedema (rare)
Harm to the fetus: stop before or as soon as pregnancy is known

cautions: Sick-day rules: pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
Not combined with an ACE inhibitor
Avoid with NSAIDs and potassium supplements
Bilateral renal artery stenosis and pregnancy: do not use
losartan.monitoring: Kidney function and potassium before starting, 1-2 weeks after each dose change, then yearly; blood pressure.

references.title: NHS: Losartan
references.section: Taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements

routes: Oral (tablets, oral suspension)
losartan.understand: Losartan blocks the action of angiotensin II, a hormone that narrows blood vessels and makes the body hold on to salt and water. With the hormone blocked, vessels relax and blood pressure falls, and the heart and kidneys are put under less strain.
losartan.mechanismDetail: Losartan and its more potent active metabolite (EXP3174) are selective, competitive antagonists at the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor. Blockade prevents angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, sodium reabsorption, sympathetic activation and the trophic effects on cardiac and vascular tissue. Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure, which underlies the reduction in proteinuria and slowing of diabetic nephropathy but also the rise in creatinine when renal perfusion depends on angiotensin II (renal artery stenosis, dehydration, NSAIDs). Because ACE is not inhibited, bradykinin is not accumulated and cough and angioedema are much less frequent than with ACE inhibitors. Losartan also has a mild uricosuric effect not shared by other ARBs.

pathway.label: Vascular smooth muscle, adrenal cortex, kidney
Angiotensin II cannot constrict vessels or release aldosterone
Lower blood pressure and glomerular pressure

indications.note: Diabetic nephropathy in type 2 diabetes with proteinuria, as part of antihypertensive treatment
Chronic heart failure when ACE inhibitors are unsuitable, initiated under specialist supervision
Also to reduce stroke risk in hypertension with left ventricular hypertrophy, and diabetic nephropathy with raised creatinine and proteinuria

warnings.text: US labelling carries a boxed warning on fetal toxicity: drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus, and losartan should be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is detected.

UK information states losartan is not recommended in pregnancy or when trying to conceive, because it can harm the baby, particularly in the second and third trimesters; a different blood-pressure medicine is used.

Angioedema (swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat) is a rare but serious reaction that needs emergency treatment; it is less common than with ACE inhibitors but still possible.

Sick-day guidance: when vomiting, diarrhoea or fever cause dehydration, UK information advises that losartan may need to be paused temporarily to protect the kidneys, restarting once eating and drinking normally.

contraindications.factor: Aliskiren in people with diabetes or eGFR below 60

Losartan exposure rises markedly in severe liver disease and the BNF advises avoiding it.

contraindications.text: A history of angioedema with a renin-angiotensin drug is a reason not to use losartan.

Standing and sitting readings at the start, then routinely; home monitoring is encouraged

foodInteractions.effect: Losartan reduces aldosterone and so reduces potassium excretion; adding potassium-rich salt substitutes can push potassium to dangerous levels.

alcohol.management: UK information states moderate alcohol is usually acceptable once settled on the dose, but it can make side effects worse in the first weeks.

supplementInteractions.effect: Raised blood potassium (hyperkalaemia), which can cause dangerous heart rhythms
supplementInteractions.management: UK information advises not taking potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium with losartan unless a doctor has advised it, with blood tests if they are used together.

lisinopril.name: Lisinopril
lisinopril.summary: An ACE inhibitor that lowers blood pressure, protects the heart after a heart attack and in heart failure, and slows kidney damage in diabetes by stopping the body making angiotensin II; taken once daily, with kidney function and potassium checked at the start.
usedFor: High blood pressure: a first-line choice for adults under 55 who are not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, and for anyone with diabetes
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, where ACE inhibitors improve symptoms and survival
After a heart attack, started within 24 hours in stable patients
Diabetic kidney disease with protein in the urine
lisinopril.howItWorks: Blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, the enzyme in the lungs and blood vessels that turns inactive angiotensin I into angiotensin II. Less angiotensin II means arteries relax, the adrenal glands release less aldosterone so the kidneys keep less salt and water, and the pressure inside the kidney's filters falls. The same enzyme normally breaks down bradykinin, so bradykinin builds up: that adds to the vessel relaxation but also causes the dry cough in about one in ten people. Unlike most ACE inhibitors lisinopril is not a prodrug and is not metabolised by the liver.
forms: Tablets 2.5, 5, 10 and 20 mg once daily; oral solution
lisinopril.onset: Blood pressure falls within hours of the first dose (which can cause first-dose hypotension); full effect after 2-4 weeks at a steady dose.

common: Dry, tickly cough (about 1 in 10; does not improve with time and is the usual reason for switching to an ARB)
Dizziness and light-headedness, particularly on standing and after the first dose
Headache, tiredness, diarrhoea
A small rise in creatinine and potassium
serious: Angioedema: swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat, which can obstruct breathing and needs emergency treatment; more common in people of Black African origin and can occur after years of treatment
Acute kidney injury with dehydration, NSAIDs or narrowed renal arteries
High potassium, especially with kidney disease, potassium supplements or spironolactone
Severe hypotension, particularly in heart failure, on diuretics or when dehydrated
Harm to the fetus: stop as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (rare liver reaction)

cautions: Sick-day rules: pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever with dehydration
Not combined with an ARB or aliskiren; never within 36 hours of sacubitril/valsartan
NSAIDs, potassium supplements and salt substitutes raise the risk of kidney injury and high potassium
Bilateral renal artery stenosis, previous angioedema, pregnancy: do not use
lisinopril.monitoring: Kidney function and potassium before starting, 1-2 weeks after starting and after each dose change, then yearly; blood pressure.

references.title: NHS: Lisinopril
references.section: Taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements

references.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

routes: Oral (tablets, oral solution)
lisinopril.understand: Lisinopril stops your body making angiotensin II, a hormone that tightens blood vessels and makes the kidneys hold on to salt and water. Without it, vessels relax and the heart pumps against less resistance, so blood pressure falls and a weak heart has an easier job.
lisinopril.mechanismDetail: Lisinopril is a lysine analogue of enalaprilat that inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme (kininase II) directly without needing hepatic activation. Reduced angiotensin II lowers arteriolar tone, aldosterone secretion, sodium retention and sympathetic drive, and dilates the efferent glomerular arteriole, lowering intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria. Accumulation of bradykinin contributes to vasodilation and to cough and angioedema. In heart failure the fall in afterload and preload and the interruption of neurohormonal activation improve symptoms and survival; after myocardial infarction, early treatment limits ventricular remodelling. Lisinopril is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so exposure rises as eGFR falls and doses are reduced accordingly.

pathway.label: Vasodilation, less aldosterone, lower glomerular pressure
Lower blood pressure, lower cardiac workload
Hypertension, heart failure, diabetic kidney disease

indications.note: Symptomatic heart failure as an adjunct to diuretics

Alone or with other medicines; also heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack

Kidney function can deteriorate, particularly with renovascular disease, heart failure, dehydration or NSAIDs; check creatinine and potassium before and 1-2 weeks after starting and after dose increases.

rosuvastatin.name: Rosuvastatin
rosuvastatin.summary: A high-intensity statin that lowers LDL cholesterol by more, milligram for milligram, than any other statin, used to prevent heart attacks and strokes when atorvastatin is not tolerated or not enough; the dose is limited by kidney function, ethnicity and interacting drugs.
usedFor: Lowering LDL cholesterol to prevent cardiovascular disease, as an alternative high-intensity statin to atorvastatin
Primary hypercholesterolaemia, mixed dyslipidaemia and familial hypercholesterolaemia, including in children from 6 years under specialist care
Slowing the progression of atherosclerosis
rosuvastatin.howItWorks: Like atorvastatin it blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls cholesterol production in the liver, so the liver takes more LDL out of the blood. Rosuvastatin is the most potent statin by weight (5-10 mg gives a similar LDL reduction to 20-40 mg of atorvastatin), is water-soluble, and is barely metabolised by the liver's CYP enzymes, so it has fewer interactions with antibiotics and antifungals; instead its levels depend on transporters and on the kidney, which is why doses are capped in kidney impairment, in people of Asian ancestry and with ciclosporin or some HIV medicines.
forms: Tablets 5, 10, 20 and 40 mg once daily at any time of day; the 40 mg dose is for specialist use only
rosuvastatin.onset: LDL cholesterol falls within a week and reaches its maximum by four weeks. Taken lifelong.

common: Muscle aches (as with other statins, most reported aches also occur on placebo)
Headache, dizziness, constipation, nausea, abdominal pain

serious: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), particularly at 40 mg, with interacting drugs, kidney impairment or hypothyroidism
Liver enzyme rise (rare, usually harmless); rare hepatitis
Protein and blood in the urine at high doses (tubular, usually transient)
Rare immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, interstitial lung disease, severe skin reactions

Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; active liver disease

rosuvastatin.monitoring: Lipids and liver tests at baseline, 3 months and 12 months; kidney function before choosing the dose; creatine kinase if muscle symptoms.

routes: Oral (tablets)
rosuvastatin.understand: Rosuvastatin blocks the enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol, so the liver takes more LDL cholesterol out of your blood. Lower LDL means less build-up in artery walls and a lower risk of heart attack and stroke.
rosuvastatin.mechanismDetail: Rosuvastatin is a hydrophilic, hepatoselective HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor taken into hepatocytes by OATP1B1. It reduces cholesterol synthesis, upregulates LDL receptors and lowers LDL cholesterol by about 45-63% across the 5-40 mg range, with larger HDL increases than other statins. Only about 10% is metabolised (mainly CYP2C9, negligibly CYP3A4), so macrolides and azole antifungals have little effect; exposure is instead raised by OATP1B1 and BCRP inhibitors (ciclosporin, gemfibrozil, some protease inhibitors) and by reduced renal function, and is about twofold higher in people of Asian ancestry because of transporter polymorphisms, hence the dose caps. High doses can cause dose-related proteinuria of tubular origin.

azithromycin.name: Azithromycin
azithromycin.summary: A macrolide antibiotic that stops bacteria making proteins, given as a short course (often three days) for chest, ear, sinus, skin and sexually transmitted infections and as an alternative in penicillin allergy; long-lasting in tissues, with cautions about heart rhythm and interactions.
usedFor: Community-acquired pneumonia and chest infections, particularly in penicillin allergy or when atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) are suspected
Ear, sinus, throat and skin infections in penicillin allergy
Chlamydia and some other sexually transmitted infections (single dose)
Long-term prophylaxis to reduce exacerbations in COPD and bronchiectasis, under specialist supervision (unlicensed use)
azithromycin.howItWorks: Binds to the bacterial ribosome (the 50S subunit) and blocks the tunnel through which new proteins leave, so the bacterium cannot make the proteins it needs to grow. Human ribosomes are built differently and are not affected. Azithromycin is concentrated inside cells, particularly white cells, which carry it to sites of infection, and it lingers in tissues for days after the last dose, which is why courses are short. Because it barely interferes with the liver's drug-metabolising enzymes, it has fewer interactions than erythromycin and clarithromycin.
forms: Capsules and tablets 250 and 500 mg, oral suspension; usually 500 mg once daily for 3 days, or a single 1 g dose for chlamydia; intravenous infusion in hospital
azithromycin.onset: Improvement expected within 2-3 days; tissue levels persist for 5-7 days after a 3-day course.

common: Diarrhoea, nausea, stomach pain, wind, loss of appetite
Headache, dizziness, altered taste
Thrush (oral or vaginal)
serious: Allergic reactions including anaphylaxis and severe skin reactions
Heart rhythm disturbance from QT prolongation, particularly with other QT-prolonging drugs, low potassium or magnesium, or existing heart rhythm problems
Liver injury (jaundice, dark urine, pale stools)
Severe or persistent diarrhoea (Clostridioides difficile infection)
Worsening of myasthenia gravis; hearing loss with long courses

cautions: Tell the prescriber about heart rhythm problems, long QT, low potassium or magnesium, and any medicine that affects heart rhythm
Liver disease and severe kidney impairment need dose consideration
Antacids containing aluminium or magnesium are taken 2 hours apart
Warfarin, digoxin and ciclosporin need extra monitoring
Long-term prophylaxis needs baseline ECG, liver tests and hearing checks
azithromycin.monitoring: Clinical response; ECG, liver function and hearing before and during long-term prophylaxis; INR if on warfarin.

routes: Oral (capsules, tablets, oral suspension); intravenous infusion; eye drops
azithromycin.understand: Azithromycin stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to grow and multiply. Your immune system then clears the weakened bacteria. It builds up inside cells and stays in the body for days, so a course can be as short as three days.
azithromycin.mechanismDetail: Azithromycin is an azalide macrolide that binds reversibly to the 23S rRNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit within the peptide exit tunnel, blocking translocation and elongation of the nascent polypeptide; the effect is mainly bacteriostatic, bactericidal against some organisms at high concentrations. It achieves intracellular and tissue concentrations many times those in plasma, is delivered by phagocytes to infected tissue and has a tissue half-life of 2-4 days, allowing 3- to 5-day courses and single-dose regimens. Its spectrum includes streptococci, Haemophilus, Moraxella, atypical respiratory pathogens (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia, Legionella), Chlamydia trachomatis and Mycobacterium avium complex; pneumococcal macrolide resistance is common in some regions. Unlike erythromycin and clarithromycin it is a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4, but it inhibits P-glycoprotein (raising digoxin levels) and, like all macrolides, can prolong the QT interval. Long-term low-dose use in COPD and bronchiectasis works partly through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.

clopidogrel.name: Clopidogrel
clopidogrel.summary: An antiplatelet medicine that stops platelets clumping by blocking their P2Y12 receptor, taken to prevent clots after a heart attack, stent, stroke or in peripheral artery disease, often alongside aspirin for a defined period.
usedFor: Preventing further events after a heart attack or acute coronary syndrome, usually with aspirin for up to 12 months
After a coronary stent, to stop the stent clotting
After an ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack, as long-term single antiplatelet treatment
Peripheral arterial disease
clopidogrel.howItWorks: Clopidogrel is a prodrug: the liver converts it, largely through the enzyme CYP2C19, into a molecule that binds irreversibly to the P2Y12 receptor on platelets. Without that receptor's signal, platelets cannot be activated by ADP and stick together far less readily. Because the block is permanent for the life of each platelet, the effect lasts about a week after stopping.
routes: Oral (tablets)
forms: Tablets 75 mg once daily; a larger loading dose is given in hospital at the start
clopidogrel.onset: Antiplatelet effect within hours of a loading dose, or over several days at the usual daily dose; lasts 5-7 days after stopping as new platelets replace the blocked ones.

common: Bleeding more easily: nosebleeds, bruising, bleeding gums, longer bleeding from cuts
Diarrhoea, stomach pain, indigestion
serious: Serious bleeding: blood in urine or stools, black stools, vomiting blood, a bleed after a head injury
Signs of an allergic reaction
Very rarely, a blood disorder causing fever, bruising and confusion (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)

cautions: Tell any doctor, dentist or pharmacist that you take it; it is usually paused before surgery only on the advice of the prescriber
Omeprazole and esomeprazole reduce its activation; other acid-suppressing medicines are preferred if one is needed
Combined with aspirin, warfarin, a DOAC or an NSAID the bleeding risk rises and the combination is decided by the prescriber
Some people convert it poorly (CYP2C19 variants) and get less protection
clopidogrel.monitoring: Signs of bleeding at every review; a full blood count if bleeding or bruising is unexplained. No routine level or test measures its effect.

bisoprolol.name: Bisoprolol
bisoprolol.summary: A once-daily beta blocker that selectively slows the heart and lowers its workload, used for heart failure, angina, high blood pressure and to control the rate in atrial fibrillation.
usedFor: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, where it improves survival
Angina
High blood pressure, usually when other classes are unsuitable or as an add-on
Rate control in atrial fibrillation and other fast rhythms
bisoprolol.howItWorks: Bisoprolol blocks beta-1 adrenoceptors on heart muscle and the conducting system, so adrenaline and noradrenaline can no longer speed the heart or make it contract as forcefully. The heart beats more slowly, needs less oxygen and, in heart failure, is protected from the long-term damage of sustained sympathetic drive. It has little effect on the beta-2 receptors of the airways at usual doses, though it is still used with caution in asthma.
routes: Oral (tablets)
forms: Tablets 1.25 to 10 mg once daily, started low and increased slowly in heart failure
bisoprolol.onset: Heart rate and blood pressure fall within hours; the benefit in heart failure builds over months. Not stopped suddenly: the dose is reduced gradually.

common: Tiredness, cold hands and feet, a slow pulse
Headache, dizziness, feeling sick
Sleep disturbance
serious: Breathlessness or wheeze, particularly in asthma
Fainting or a very slow heartbeat
Worsening fluid retention early in heart failure treatment
Signs of an allergic reaction

cautions: Avoided in asthma unless a specialist judges the benefit greater; used cautiously in COPD
Not started during decompensated heart failure; introduced once the person is stable
Combined with verapamil or diltiazem it can slow the heart dangerously
Masks the warning signs of low blood sugar in diabetes
Never stopped abruptly: the dose is tapered
bisoprolol.monitoring: Heart rate and blood pressure at each dose change; symptoms of heart failure and fluid retention during titration; blood glucose awareness in diabetes.

citalopram.name: Citalopram
citalopram.summary: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor antidepressant used for depression and panic disorder, taken once daily, with a maximum dose set by its effect on the heart's QT interval.
usedFor: Depression
Panic disorder
Also used for some anxiety disorders under specialist advice
citalopram.howItWorks: Citalopram blocks the serotonin transporter that carries serotonin back into the nerve ending after it has been released, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and signalling through serotonin receptors increases. Mood and anxiety improve gradually over several weeks as receptor sensitivity and downstream signalling adapt; the immediate rise in serotonin explains the early nausea and restlessness.
routes: Oral (tablets, oral drops)
forms: Tablets 10, 20 and 40 mg once daily; oral drops (a different strength equivalence from tablets)
citalopram.onset: Benefit usually within 4 to 6 weeks; side effects appear first. Reduced gradually at the end of treatment to avoid discontinuation symptoms.

common: Feeling sick, dry mouth, sweating, tiredness
Difficulty sleeping, feeling restless or shaky
Reduced appetite, weight change, sexual problems
serious: Thoughts of self-harm, especially in the first weeks and under 25 years of age
Palpitations or fainting from a prolonged QT interval, more likely at higher doses or with other QT-prolonging medicines
Bleeding, particularly with NSAIDs, aspirin or anticoagulants
Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic medicines: agitation, fever, muscle twitching
Low sodium, especially in older people

cautions: Maximum daily dose is lower in people over 65 and in liver impairment because of the QT effect
Not combined with other QT-prolonging medicines or with MAOI antidepressants
Bleeding risk rises with NSAIDs, aspirin and anticoagulants
Closer monitoring for suicidal thoughts when starting, especially in young people
Serotonin syndrome risk with tramadol, triptans, St John's wort and other serotonergic medicines
citalopram.monitoring: Mood and suicidal thoughts in the first weeks of treatment and after dose changes; an ECG before or during treatment in people with heart disease or on other QT-prolonging medicines; sodium in older people if drowsy or confused.

clarithromycin.name: Clarithromycin
clarithromycin.summary: A macrolide antibiotic for chest, skin, ear and throat infections and part of the combination that eradicates Helicobacter pylori, notable for the number of medicines it interacts with through CYP3A4.
usedFor: Chest infections including pneumonia, and exacerbations of COPD
Skin and soft-tissue infections, ear, sinus and throat infections, particularly in people allergic to penicillin
Helicobacter pylori eradication, with a proton-pump inhibitor and a second antibiotic
Some mycobacterial infections under specialist care
clarithromycin.howItWorks: Clarithromycin binds the 50S subunit of the bacterial ribosome and stops the growing protein chain from moving along, so the bacteria cannot make the proteins they need; it slows their growth and, at higher concentrations, kills some species. It concentrates inside cells and lung tissue, which suits it to respiratory infections. In the liver it strongly inhibits CYP3A4, the enzyme that clears many other medicines.
routes: Oral (tablets, modified-release tablets, oral suspension); intravenous infusion
forms: Tablets 250 and 500 mg twice daily, or 500 mg modified-release once daily; oral suspension; intravenous infusion in hospital
clarithromycin.onset: Symptoms usually improve within a few days; the full course is completed to prevent relapse and resistance.

common: Feeling sick, diarrhoea, stomach pain, bloating
A changed sense of taste
Headache, difficulty sleeping
serious: Severe or persistent diarrhoea (possible C. difficile infection)
Palpitations or fainting from a prolonged QT interval
Yellowing of the skin or eyes, pale stools, dark urine
Severe skin reactions or an allergic reaction
Hearing loss or ringing in the ears, usually reversible

cautions: Interacts with many medicines through CYP3A4: statins (simvastatin and atorvastatin), warfarin, some calcium-channel blockers, colchicine, some antipsychotics and anticoagulants, among others
Not combined with other QT-prolonging medicines where an alternative exists
Dose reduced in significant kidney impairment
Liver disease and a history of jaundice with a macrolide
Myasthenia gravis can worsen
clarithromycin.monitoring: No routine tests for short courses; INR closely if on warfarin; muscle symptoms if on a statin; an ECG if heart disease or other QT-prolonging medicines.

tramadol.name: Tramadol
tramadol.summary: An opioid painkiller for moderate to severe pain that also boosts serotonin and noradrenaline signalling, a controlled drug with a particular risk of seizures and serotonin syndrome when combined with antidepressants.
tramadol.class: Opioid analgesic (weak opioid with serotonergic and noradrenergic activity)
usedFor: Moderate to severe pain, including after surgery or injury, when non-opioid painkillers are not enough
Short-term use is preferred; long-term use for chronic non-cancer pain is discouraged
tramadol.howItWorks: Tramadol and, more strongly, the active metabolite the liver makes from it through CYP2D6, act on mu-opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord to dampen pain signalling. Unlike other opioids it also blocks the reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline, which adds to pain relief but is why it can cause serotonin syndrome with antidepressants and lowers the seizure threshold. People who lack CYP2D6 activity get less pain relief; ultra-rapid metabolisers get more opioid effect.
routes: Oral (capsules, tablets, modified-release tablets and capsules, oral drops); injection
forms: Capsules 50 mg, modified-release tablets and capsules 12- or 24-hourly, orodispersible tablets, oral drops; injection in hospital
tramadol.onset: Pain relief within about an hour; modified-release forms last 12 or 24 hours.

common: Feeling sick or being sick, constipation, dry mouth
Dizziness, drowsiness, headache, tiredness
Sweating, feeling agitated
serious: Slow or shallow breathing, extreme drowsiness, especially with alcohol, benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids
Seizures, more likely at high doses or with antidepressants and other seizure-threshold-lowering medicines
Serotonin syndrome with antidepressants, triptans or St John's wort
Dependence, withdrawal on stopping, and misuse
Signs of an allergic reaction

cautions: A controlled drug: prescribed for the shortest time and reviewed regularly
Not combined with MAOI antidepressants; caution with SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and other serotonergic medicines
Alcohol, benzodiazepines and other sedatives increase respiratory depression
Epilepsy or a low seizure threshold
Reduced doses or avoidance in severe kidney or liver impairment; carbamazepine reduces its effect
Driving: it is an offence in the UK to drive with the ability impaired by tramadol
tramadol.monitoring: Pain relief and function, sedation and breathing, constipation and signs of dependence at each review; kidney and liver function in long-term use.

oxycodone.name: Oxycodone
oxycodone.summary: A strong opioid painkiller for severe pain, including cancer pain and pain after major surgery, available in immediate- and modified-release forms and as a controlled drug with the full opioid risks of dependence and respiratory depression.
usedFor: Severe pain that non-opioid painkillers and weaker opioids do not control
Cancer pain and palliative care
Pain after major surgery
Long-term use for chronic non-cancer pain is discouraged because benefit is limited and harm accumulates
oxycodone.howItWorks: Oxycodone is a full agonist at mu-opioid receptors in the brain and spinal cord. Activating them closes the gates on pain signals travelling up the spinal cord and changes how the brain experiences pain, while also slowing breathing, dulling alertness, causing constipation and, with repeated use, producing tolerance and dependence. It is metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4 and CYP2D6) and cleared by the kidneys, so both organs affect its dose.
routes: Oral (immediate-release capsules and liquid, modified-release tablets); injection
forms: Immediate-release capsules and oral liquid every 4-6 hours; modified-release tablets every 12 hours; injections and syringe-driver infusions in hospital and palliative care
oxycodone.onset: Immediate-release forms work within about 30 minutes and last 4-6 hours; modified-release tablets last 12 hours.

common: Constipation, feeling sick, being sick
Drowsiness, dizziness, confusion
Dry mouth, itching, sweating, headache
serious: Slow or shallow breathing and extreme drowsiness, particularly with alcohol, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids or other sedatives
Dependence, tolerance and withdrawal symptoms on stopping
Very low blood pressure, fainting
Severe constipation with bowel obstruction
Signs of an allergic reaction

cautions: A controlled drug: prescribed at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a plan for stopping
Alcohol, benzodiazepines and other sedatives can cause fatal respiratory depression together
Dose reduced in kidney or liver impairment and in older or frail people
CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, some antifungals) raise its levels; inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine) lower them
Modified-release tablets are swallowed whole; crushing releases the whole dose at once
Driving: illegal in the UK if driving is impaired
oxycodone.monitoring: Pain relief, sedation, breathing rate and constipation at every review; kidney and liver function; regular reassessment of the need to continue, with a tapering plan.

chlorphenamine.name: Chlorphenamine
chlorphenamine.summary: A first-generation antihistamine, sold over the counter, that relieves hay fever, hives and allergic reactions within an hour but causes drowsiness because it enters the brain; also given by injection for severe allergic reactions.
usedFor: Hay fever and other allergic rhinitis
Hives (urticaria), itchy rashes and insect bites
Symptom relief in allergic reactions and, by injection, as an adjunct in anaphylaxis after adrenaline
Some cold and flu remedies contain it for its drying effect
chlorphenamine.howItWorks: Chlorphenamine blocks H1 histamine receptors, so the histamine released by mast cells in an allergic reaction can no longer widen small blood vessels, make them leaky or trigger itch and sneezing. Because it crosses into the brain and also blocks some muscarinic receptors, it causes drowsiness, dry mouth and blurred vision, which newer antihistamines largely avoid.
routes: Oral (tablets, oral solution); injection
forms: Tablets 4 mg every 4-6 hours (maximum daily dose applies), oral solution for children over the licensed age; injection in hospital

common: Drowsiness and slowed reactions
Dry mouth, blurred vision, difficulty passing urine
Headache, feeling sick
serious: Confusion, agitation or falls, particularly in older people
Palpitations or a fast heartbeat
Signs of an allergic reaction to the medicine itself

cautions: Do not drive, cycle or operate machinery if drowsy; alcohol and other sedatives add to the effect
Avoided in older people where possible (falls, confusion) and in glaucoma, prostate enlargement and urinary retention
Not for children under the licensed age without medical advice
Adds sedation to opioids, benzodiazepines and some antidepressants
chlorphenamine.monitoring: No tests; drowsiness, urinary symptoms and confusion are reviewed, especially in older people.
