total-cholesterol.name: Total cholesterol
total-cholesterol.summary: The sum of all the cholesterol carried in blood by lipoproteins: LDL, HDL and the remainder. One line of a lipid profile, useful mainly as the starting point for the ratios and the non-HDL value that guide cardiovascular risk assessment.
total-cholesterol.what: Cholesterol is a waxy molecule every cell needs for its membranes and for making steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. It does not dissolve in water, so it travels in blood packaged with proteins as lipoproteins. The total is dominated by LDL cholesterol, the fraction deposited in artery walls, and HDL cholesterol, the fraction being carried back to the liver. A high total is therefore not always harmful (a large HDL share is protective) and a normal total can hide a poor pattern, which is why risk calculators use the ratio of total to HDL and guidelines increasingly track non-HDL cholesterol instead.
higher: Diet high in saturated fat, excess weight, inactivity
Familial hypercholesterolaemia and other inherited lipid disorders
Hypothyroidism, kidney disease with heavy proteinuria, cholestatic liver disease
Pregnancy; some medicines (corticosteroids, some antiretrovirals, isotretinoin)
lower: Hyperthyroidism, malnutrition, malabsorption
Severe acute illness, cancer, advanced liver disease
Lipid-lowering treatment
factors: Acute illness, surgery and heart attack lower cholesterol for several weeks
Weight change, alcohol and pregnancy
Fasting is no longer required for most purposes but changes triglycerides more than cholesterol
total-cholesterol.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

ldl-cholesterol.name: LDL cholesterol
ldl-cholesterol.summary: The cholesterol carried by low-density lipoprotein, the particle that deposits cholesterol in artery walls and drives atherosclerosis. The main target of statin treatment and the lipid value most closely tied to heart attack and stroke risk.
ldl-cholesterol.what: The liver packages triglycerides and cholesterol into VLDL particles; as tissues strip out the triglyceride, the particles shrink into cholesterol-rich LDL. LDL delivers cholesterol to cells through LDL receptors, but when particles are numerous or the artery wall is damaged they enter the wall, are oxidised and are engulfed by macrophages that become the foam cells of a fatty plaque. Statins lower LDL by making the liver display more LDL receptors. Laboratories usually calculate LDL from total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides (the Friedewald equation), which becomes unreliable when triglycerides are high; non-HDL cholesterol (total minus HDL) avoids that problem and is the value UK guidance uses for treatment targets.
ldl-cholesterol.unit: mmol/L (UK) or mg/dL (US); usually calculated rather than measured directly

Saturated-fat-rich diet, obesity, inactivity
Hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, diabetes
Some medicines (corticosteroids, ciclosporin, some antipsychotics)
lower: Lipid-lowering treatment (statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors)
Hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, severe illness, advanced liver disease
Rare inherited disorders of lipoprotein synthesis
factors: Very high triglycerides make the calculated LDL invalid
Acute illness lowers the level for weeks
Fasting state changes the triglyceride input to the calculation
ldl-cholesterol.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

hdl-cholesterol.name: HDL cholesterol
hdl-cholesterol.summary: The cholesterol carried by high-density lipoprotein, the particle that collects cholesterol from tissues and artery walls and returns it to the liver. A higher level is associated with lower cardiovascular risk and enters the standard risk calculators.
hdl-cholesterol.what: HDL particles are made by the liver and gut and pick up cholesterol from peripheral cells, including the foam cells of a developing plaque, delivering it back to the liver for excretion in bile (reverse cholesterol transport). Population studies show a steady fall in heart disease as HDL rises, so it appears in risk scores such as QRISK as the total-to-HDL ratio. Drugs that raise HDL have not, however, reduced heart attacks in trials, so HDL is read as a risk marker rather than a treatment target. Exercise, weight loss, stopping smoking and moderate alcohol raise it; obesity, inactivity, smoking, type 2 diabetes and high triglycerides lower it.

lower: Obesity, physical inactivity, smoking
Type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides, metabolic syndrome
Anabolic steroids, some beta blockers and progestogens
Rare inherited HDL deficiencies

Acute illness
Menopause and hormone treatment

triglycerides.name: Triglycerides
triglycerides.summary: The main form in which fat is stored and transported: three fatty acids on a glycerol backbone, carried in blood by chylomicrons after meals and by VLDL from the liver. Raised levels add to cardiovascular risk and very high levels can trigger pancreatitis.
triglycerides.what: After a fatty meal the gut packages triglyceride into chylomicrons, which is why a non-fasting sample reads higher and why laboratories once insisted on fasting. Between meals the liver exports triglyceride in VLDL, particularly when it is over-supplied with calories, alcohol or sugar, or when insulin resistance lets fat stores release fatty acids freely. Moderately raised triglycerides usually travel with low HDL, central obesity and prediabetes; levels above about 10 mmol/L carry a real risk of acute pancreatitis. Because triglyceride-rich particles contribute to non-HDL cholesterol, the lipid profile as a whole rather than the single number guides treatment.

Obesity, type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome
Hypothyroidism, kidney disease, pregnancy
Medicines: corticosteroids, oestrogens, isotretinoin, some antipsychotics, thiazides, beta blockers
Inherited hypertriglyceridaemia (familial chylomicronaemia, familial combined hyperlipidaemia)
lower: Malnutrition, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism
Fibrates, omega-3 preparations, statins to a lesser degree, weight loss

Alcohol in the preceding days
Acute illness and pregnancy

alt.name: ALT (alanine aminotransferase)
alt.summary: An enzyme concentrated in liver cells that leaks into blood when they are injured. The most liver-specific of the routine liver blood tests and the one that rises first in fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis and drug-induced injury.
alt.what: ALT sits in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes, where it shuttles amino groups between amino acids as part of energy metabolism. Damage to the cell membrane releases it into the circulation, so the level rises with hepatocellular injury of any cause: viral hepatitis, alcohol, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis, drugs and toxins, or a congested liver in heart failure. Because ALT is mostly confined to the liver it is more specific than AST, and the ratio between the two helps distinguish alcohol-related disease (AST higher) from other causes (ALT higher). A mildly raised ALT is common and often reflects fatty liver; a level many times the upper limit points to acute hepatitis, ischaemia or paracetamol toxicity.
alt.unit: U/L (units per litre); reference limits differ by laboratory and sex

Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, E), glandular fever
Alcohol; medicines such as paracetamol in overdose, statins, antibiotics, antiepileptics, methotrexate
Autoimmune hepatitis, haemochromatosis, Wilson disease, coeliac disease
Ischaemic liver injury, heart failure with congestion, bile-duct obstruction (with ALP)
Strenuous exercise and muscle injury (smaller effect than on AST)

ast.name: AST (aspartate aminotransferase)
ast.summary: An enzyme found in liver cells but also in heart, skeletal muscle, kidney, brain and red cells. It rises with liver injury alongside ALT, and the AST:ALT ratio helps point towards or away from alcohol-related liver disease.
ast.what: AST is present both in the cytoplasm and in the mitochondria of cells, and it is far less specific to the liver than ALT. In hepatocellular injury both enzymes rise; in alcohol-related liver disease AST is typically higher than ALT (a ratio above 2), partly because alcohol depletes the vitamin B6 that ALT needs and damages mitochondria. Muscle injury, a heart attack, haemolysis and vigorous exercise all raise AST with little change in ALT, so an isolated AST elevation prompts a creatine kinase test. In advanced fibrosis the ratio flips because ALT production falls, which is why AST-based scores (such as APRI and FIB-4) are used to estimate scarring.

Alcohol-related liver disease (AST greater than ALT)
Muscle disease or injury, rhabdomyolysis, strenuous exercise, seizures
Heart attack, haemolysis, pancreatitis, coeliac disease
Cirrhosis with advanced fibrosis (AST:ALT ratio rises)

alp.name: ALP (alkaline phosphatase)
alp.summary: An enzyme made mainly by the cells lining the bile ducts and by bone-forming cells. A raised level with a raised GGT points to obstructed bile flow (cholestasis); a raised level with a normal GGT points to bone, growth or pregnancy.
alp.what: Alkaline phosphatase is anchored to the membranes of bile-duct cells, osteoblasts in bone, the placenta and the gut lining. When bile flow is obstructed, by a gallstone in the common bile duct, a tumour of the pancreas head or bile ducts, or by drugs that impair bile secretion, the liver makes far more ALP and releases it into blood. Growing children and adolescents have naturally high bone ALP, as do people healing a fracture, and the placenta raises it in the third trimester of pregnancy. Distinguishing liver from bone ALP relies on the GGT (raised only in the liver pattern) or on measuring the separate isoenzymes.
alp.unit: U/L (units per litre); much higher in growing children

Liver infiltration or abscess, cirrhosis, some drugs (for example flucloxacillin, co-amoxiclav)
Bone: Paget disease, fracture healing, osteomalacia, bone metastases, hyperparathyroidism
Growth in childhood and adolescence, third-trimester pregnancy
lower: Hypophosphatasia (rare inherited deficiency)
Hypothyroidism, zinc or magnesium deficiency, malnutrition, some anaemias

ggt.name: GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase)
ggt.summary: A membrane enzyme of bile-duct and liver cells that rises with cholestasis, alcohol and many medicines. On its own it is too non-specific to diagnose anything, but it confirms that a raised alkaline phosphatase comes from the liver rather than bone.
ggt.what: GGT transfers amino acid fragments across cell membranes and is abundant in the biliary tree, liver, kidney and pancreas. Its main practical value is as a companion to ALP: both rise in bile-duct obstruction, whereas ALP alone rises in bone disease and pregnancy. GGT is also induced by alcohol and by enzyme-inducing drugs such as phenytoin and carbamazepine, so a raised GGT with otherwise normal tests often reflects drinking, obesity or medication rather than liver damage. It does not fall quickly after stopping alcohol, taking several weeks to normalise.

Alcohol use, especially regular heavy drinking
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes
Enzyme-inducing medicines (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin), some others
Pancreatitis, heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
lower: No clinical significance; low in some inherited conditions

Medicines
Body weight

bilirubin.name: Bilirubin
bilirubin.summary: The yellow pigment made when old red cells are broken down, processed by the liver and excreted in bile. A high level causes jaundice; whether the excess is unconjugated or conjugated tells whether the problem lies before the liver, inside it or in the bile ducts.
bilirubin.what: About 1% of red cells are retired every day, and their haemoglobin is converted into unconjugated bilirubin, which travels bound to albumin to the liver. Hepatocytes attach glucuronic acid to make water-soluble conjugated bilirubin and secrete it into bile, where it gives stools their colour. Excess unconjugated bilirubin means too much production (haemolysis) or slow conjugation (newborns, Gilbert syndrome); excess conjugated bilirubin means damaged hepatocytes or blocked bile ducts, and it spills into urine, turning it dark. Jaundice becomes visible in the whites of the eyes and skin once the total rises above roughly 40 to 50 µmol/L. In newborns very high levels can injure the brain, so bilirubin is monitored closely in the first days of life.
higher: Haemolysis: haemolytic anaemias, transfusion reactions, large bruises (unconjugated)
Gilbert syndrome, a common harmless inherited slowing of conjugation (unconjugated, rises with fasting and illness)
Hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug-induced liver injury (mixed)
Bile-duct obstruction by stones, strictures or tumours, primary biliary cholangitis (conjugated)
Newborn jaundice
lower: No clinical significance
factors: Fasting and intercurrent illness raise unconjugated bilirubin in Gilbert syndrome
Haemolysed samples and exposure of the sample to light
Some medicines interfere with the assay or with excretion
bilirubin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

albumin.name: Albumin
albumin.summary: The most abundant protein in blood, made by the liver. It keeps fluid inside the vessels and carries hormones, drugs, calcium and bilirubin. A low level is common in serious illness and reflects inflammation, loss or poor liver synthesis rather than any one disease.
albumin.what: Albumin holds water in the circulation by osmotic pull; when it falls, fluid leaks into tissues and causes oedema and ascites. The liver makes about 10 to 15 grams a day and the protein lasts about three weeks in the circulation, so albumin is a slow measure of synthetic function and falls late in liver disease. Far more often a low albumin reflects the acute-phase response (the liver switches to making inflammatory proteins such as CRP during infection, surgery or cancer), losses through the kidney (nephrotic syndrome) or gut, malnutrition, or dilution by intravenous fluids. Because many drugs and about half of blood calcium ride on albumin, laboratories report a calcium value adjusted for it.
higher: Dehydration (concentration of the blood) is the only common cause of a genuinely high value
lower: Acute and chronic inflammation, infection, sepsis, surgery, cancer
Cirrhosis and other severe liver disease
Nephrotic syndrome (loss in urine), protein-losing enteropathy, burns
Malnutrition and malabsorption
Heart failure, pregnancy, intravenous fluid dilution, older age
factors: Posture (lying down lowers it slightly), tourniquet time and hydration
Acute illness at the time of sampling
Pregnancy
albumin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

creatinine.name: Creatinine
creatinine.summary: A waste product of muscle metabolism produced at a steady rate and cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. The rise in blood creatinine when filtration falls makes it the everyday marker of kidney function and the input for the eGFR calculation.
creatinine.what: Muscle cells store energy as creatine phosphate, and a fixed fraction breaks down each day into creatinine, which the glomeruli filter freely and the tubules barely reabsorb. When the glomerular filtration rate falls, creatinine accumulates, but the relationship is curved: filtration can halve before creatinine leaves the reference interval, and small rises at low values mean large losses of function. Because production depends on muscle mass, a frail older person and a muscular young athlete have different normal values for the same kidney function, which is why laboratories convert creatinine into an estimated GFR that accounts for age and sex. A rising creatinine over hours to days defines acute kidney injury; a persistently reduced eGFR over three months defines chronic kidney disease.
higher: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, shock, obstruction, nephrotoxic drugs, contrast
Chronic kidney disease from diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease and others
Large muscle mass, creatine supplements, a large meat meal, muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis)
Medicines that block tubular secretion without harming the kidney (trimethoprim, cimetidine), and ACE inhibitors or ARBs starting (a small expected rise)
lower: Low muscle mass: older age, frailty, amputation, muscle-wasting disease
Pregnancy (higher filtration), liver disease, malnutrition
factors: Muscle mass, sex, age and ethnicity affect the value for a given filtration rate
Cooked meat, creatine supplements and intense exercise in the previous day
Hydration; some medicines
Assay standardisation between laboratories
creatinine.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

egfr.name: eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate)
egfr.summary: An estimate of how many millilitres of blood the kidneys filter each minute, calculated from creatinine together with age and sex. The number used to stage chronic kidney disease and to adjust drug doses.
egfr.what: The glomerular filtration rate is the best overall measure of kidney function but cannot be measured directly in routine care, so laboratories estimate it from serum creatinine using equations (the CKD-EPI equation in current UK and US practice; the 2021 version no longer includes a race term) that adjust for age and sex. The result is expressed per 1.73 m² of body surface area. An eGFR persistently below 60 for more than three months, or any value with markers of kidney damage such as albumin in the urine, defines chronic kidney disease, staged from G1 to G5. The estimate is least reliable at extremes of muscle mass, in pregnancy, in acute illness where creatinine is still changing, and near the normal range, where a cystatin C-based estimate can confirm the finding.
higher: A high value is normal in young adults and in pregnancy; falsely high estimates occur with low muscle mass (the equation assumes average muscle)
lower: Chronic kidney disease of any cause (diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidneys, obstruction)
Acute kidney injury (the estimate lags behind the true fall because creatinine takes time to accumulate)
Falsely low with high muscle mass, creatine supplements, a recent meat meal, or drugs that block creatinine secretion
factors: Everything that changes creatinine independently of filtration
Which equation the laboratory uses
Steady-state assumption: the estimate is invalid while kidney function is changing rapidly
egfr.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

urea.name: Urea
urea.summary: The nitrogen-containing waste the liver makes from protein breakdown, cleared by the kidneys. Reported as urea in the UK and as blood urea nitrogen (BUN) in the United States, it rises with kidney impairment but also with dehydration, bleeding into the gut and a high-protein diet.
urea.what: Ammonia released when amino acids are broken down is toxic, so the liver converts it into urea, which the kidneys filter; unlike creatinine, a good deal of urea is reabsorbed in the tubules, and more is reabsorbed when the body is dry. Urea therefore rises out of proportion to creatinine in dehydration, heart failure with poor kidney perfusion and gastrointestinal bleeding (digested blood is a protein load), and it falls in liver failure and malnutrition. Read alongside creatinine, the urea-to-creatinine pattern helps sort out whether a kidney problem is pre-renal (poor blood supply) or intrinsic. Very high urea in advanced kidney failure contributes to the nausea, itching and drowsiness of uraemia.
urea.unit: mmol/L (urea, UK) or mg/dL (BUN, US); urea 1 mmol/L ≈ BUN 2.8 mg/dL
higher: Kidney impairment, acute or chronic
Dehydration, heart failure, shock (reduced kidney perfusion)
Gastrointestinal bleeding, high-protein diet, corticosteroids, tissue breakdown
Urinary obstruction
lower: Severe liver disease (less urea made)
Malnutrition, low-protein diet, pregnancy
Over-hydration; some inherited enzyme defects
factors: Hydration and protein intake
Corticosteroids and tetracyclines
Recent gut bleeding
urea.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

potassium.name: Potassium
potassium.summary: The main positively charged ion inside cells; only about 2% is in the blood, but that small fraction sets the electrical excitability of nerves, muscle and above all the heart. Both high and low levels can cause dangerous heart rhythms.
potassium.what: The kidney matches potassium excretion to intake under the control of aldosterone, and insulin and adrenaline shift potassium into cells, which is why a rapid change in blood level can occur without any change in total body stores. Hyperkalaemia is most often a combination of reduced kidney excretion and medicines that block aldosterone or the renin-angiotensin system (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, potassium supplements); it flattens the heart's electrical recovery and can cause cardiac arrest, so a very high result is treated as an emergency and checked with an ECG. Hypokalaemia comes from losses through vomiting, diarrhoea or loop and thiazide diuretics and causes weakness, cramps and arrhythmias, particularly in people taking digoxin. Because red cells are full of potassium, a squeezed, delayed or haemolysed sample reads falsely high.
higher: Kidney impairment, acute or chronic
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone and other potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, potassium supplements and salt substitutes
Addison disease (aldosterone deficiency)
Tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis), acidosis, insulin deficiency in diabetic ketoacidosis
Spurious: haemolysed or delayed samples, very high platelet or white-cell counts
lower: Vomiting, diarrhoea, laxative misuse
Loop and thiazide diuretics, corticosteroids, high-dose salbutamol, insulin treatment
Low magnesium, Conn syndrome (aldosterone excess), Cushing syndrome
Poor intake, refeeding, alkalosis
factors: Sample handling: fist clenching, tourniquet time, delay before separation, haemolysis
Recent insulin, salbutamol or intravenous fluids
Kidney function and current medicines
potassium.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

sodium.name: Sodium
sodium.summary: The main positively charged ion of the fluid outside cells and the chief determinant of blood osmolality. Its blood level says more about the body's water balance than about salt: a low sodium usually means too much water relative to salt, a high one too little water.
sodium.what: Total body sodium sets the volume of the extracellular fluid, but the concentration in blood is regulated by thirst and by antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which tells the kidney how much water to retain. Hyponatraemia, the commonest electrolyte abnormality in hospital, arises when ADH is released inappropriately (illness, pain, some drugs, lung and brain disease), when thiazide diuretics or adrenal failure waste salt, or when heart, liver or kidney failure retain water in excess of salt. A fall that develops quickly swells brain cells and causes confusion, seizures and coma. Hypernatraemia reflects water loss that has not been replaced (fever, diarrhoea, diabetes insipidus) in people who cannot drink enough, typically the very young, the very old and the unwell. Correction in either direction must be gradual to avoid brain injury.
higher: Water loss without replacement: fever, sweating, diarrhoea, osmotic diuresis in uncontrolled diabetes, diabetes insipidus
Inability to drink: infancy, dementia, unconsciousness
Excess salt intake or hypertonic fluids (rare)
lower: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH): lung and brain disease, cancers, pain, nausea, medicines such as SSRIs, carbamazepine, antipsychotics
Thiazide diuretics
Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome (dilution)
Adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism
Excess water intake, prolonged endurance exercise with water only
Spurious (pseudohyponatraemia) with very high lipids or proteins, or a sample drawn near a drip
factors: Fluid intake and intravenous fluids at the time of sampling
Glucose: very high blood glucose lowers the measured sodium
Medicines, especially diuretics and antidepressants
sodium.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

tsh.name: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
tsh.summary: The pituitary hormone that drives the thyroid gland. Because the pituitary responds to tiny changes in thyroid hormone, TSH moves in the opposite direction to thyroid function and is the single most sensitive test of thyroid status.
tsh.what: The hypothalamus releases TRH, the pituitary responds with TSH, and TSH tells the thyroid to make thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); T4 and T3 then feed back to switch TSH off. When the thyroid fails, T4 falls and TSH climbs, often to many times the upper limit; when the thyroid is overactive, TSH is suppressed towards zero. The relationship is logarithmic, so TSH changes a great deal for a small change in T4, which is why it is the screening test and the value used to adjust levothyroxine. It takes about six weeks to settle after a dose change. TSH is unreliable when the pituitary itself is diseased, in the recovery phase of severe illness, and in the first trimester of pregnancy, when the placental hormone hCG mimics it.
higher: Primary hypothyroidism: autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, after thyroid surgery or radioiodine, iodine deficiency
Under-replacement with levothyroxine, or poor absorption of it (taken with food, iron, calcium, PPIs)
Subclinical hypothyroidism (raised TSH with normal free T4)
Recovery from severe illness, some medicines (amiodarone, lithium), rarely a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour
lower: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules, thyroiditis
Over-replacement with levothyroxine
Pituitary or hypothalamic disease (secondary hypothyroidism: low TSH with low T4)
First trimester of pregnancy, severe non-thyroidal illness, high-dose steroids and dopamine
factors: Time of day (highest overnight), acute illness, pregnancy
Biotin supplements interfere with some assays
Levothyroxine dose timing and adherence
Age: the reference interval rises in older adults
tsh.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

free-t4.name: Free T4 (thyroxine)
free-t4.summary: The unbound fraction of thyroxine, the main hormone the thyroid gland secretes. Measured with TSH, it tells whether a thyroid problem is mild or severe and whether it originates in the thyroid or the pituitary.
free-t4.what: The thyroid releases mostly T4, with a smaller amount of the more active T3; tissues convert T4 to T3 as needed. Over 99% of T4 travels bound to carrier proteins, so laboratories measure the free fraction, which is what acts on cells and is not distorted by pregnancy or the pill, both of which raise the binding proteins. A low free T4 with a high TSH is primary hypothyroidism; a low free T4 with a low or normal TSH points to pituitary disease; a high free T4 with a suppressed TSH is hyperthyroidism. Free T4 changes more quickly than TSH after starting or adjusting treatment and is the value followed in pituitary disease, where TSH cannot be trusted.
higher: Hyperthyroidism (Graves disease, toxic nodular goitre, thyroiditis)
Excess levothyroxine
Amiodarone, heparin (assay effect), biotin interference, acute psychiatric illness (transient)
Rare TSH-secreting pituitary tumours or thyroid hormone resistance
lower: Primary hypothyroidism
Pituitary or hypothalamic disease
Severe non-thyroidal illness (sick euthyroid pattern), some antiepileptic drugs and high-dose steroids
Under-treatment or malabsorption of levothyroxine
factors: Timing of the levothyroxine dose (a sample soon after a dose reads higher)
Biotin and some antibodies interfere with immunoassays
Severe illness, pregnancy (trimester-specific ranges)
free-t4.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

crp.name: C-reactive protein (CRP)
crp.summary: A protein the liver pours into blood within hours of any significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury. It rises and falls fast, so it tracks the course of an illness and the response to treatment; it does not say what the cause is.
crp.what: CRP is an acute-phase protein: interleukin-6 released at a site of inflammation tells the liver to make it, levels begin to rise within about six hours, peak at around two days and fall with a half-life of roughly 19 hours once the trigger is removed. Bacterial infection, major surgery, trauma, heart attack, flares of inflammatory arthritis or bowel disease and some cancers all raise it, often into the hundreds of mg/L; many viral infections and some autoimmune diseases such as lupus raise it only modestly. A high-sensitivity assay (hs-CRP) measures the low-grade inflammation of obesity and atherosclerosis, used in some cardiovascular risk scores. CRP responds faster than the ESR, which is why it is preferred for monitoring acute illness.
higher: Bacterial infection, sepsis, abscess, pneumonia, pyelonephritis
Surgery, trauma, burns, myocardial infarction
Inflammatory arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, vasculitis, gout flares
Cancer, particularly lymphoma and widespread disease
Mild elevation: obesity, smoking, diabetes, low-grade chronic inflammation
lower: A low value is normal; it makes significant bacterial infection or major inflammation less likely but does not exclude early infection, viral illness or localised infection
factors: Time since the illness began (a sample within the first hours can be normal)
Corticosteroids and other immunosuppressants blunt the rise
Obesity and smoking raise the baseline
Pregnancy and oestrogens raise it slightly
crp.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

ferritin.name: Ferritin
ferritin.summary: The protein that stores iron inside cells; the small amount in blood mirrors the body's iron reserve. A low ferritin is the most reliable single sign of iron deficiency, but because ferritin is also an acute-phase protein, inflammation can hide a deficiency by pushing it into the normal range.
ferritin.what: Most of the body's iron is in haemoglobin, and the rest is held in the liver, spleen and bone marrow wrapped in ferritin. Serum ferritin falls as those stores are drained, before the haemoglobin drops, so it detects iron deficiency at an early stage; a value below about 30 µg/L confirms depleted stores in an adult. Ferritin rises with inflammation, infection, liver disease, cancer and alcohol whether or not iron is present, so in someone with a raised CRP a 'normal' ferritin can still coexist with deficiency, and transferrin saturation or a trial of iron may be needed. Very high ferritin points to iron overload (haemochromatosis, repeated transfusions) or to severe inflammatory states.
higher: Inflammation and infection (acute-phase response), rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease
Liver disease, alcohol excess, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
Haemochromatosis and iron overload from transfusions
Cancer, especially lymphoma and leukaemia; very high values in adult Still disease and haemophagocytic syndromes
Metabolic syndrome, obesity
lower: Iron deficiency from blood loss (menstrual, gastrointestinal), poor intake, malabsorption (coeliac disease, gastric surgery), pregnancy and growth
Hypothyroidism and vitamin C deficiency (small effect)
factors: Any concurrent inflammation raises it independently of iron stores
Time of day, alcohol, liver disease
Recent iron infusion or transfusion
ferritin.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

inr.name: INR
inr.summary: The prothrombin time expressed as a standardised ratio, the number used to dose warfarin and to gauge the liver's production of clotting factors.
inr.what: The INR standardises the prothrombin time so that a result means the same in every laboratory. It rises when the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX and X) fall, whether because warfarin blocks their activation or because a damaged liver makes less of them.
higher: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists
Liver disease and failure
Vitamin K deficiency, including in newborns and with malabsorption
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
Interacting medicines that potentiate warfarin
lower: A warfarin dose that is too low or doses missed
High vitamin K intake
Medicines that induce warfarin metabolism
factors: An under-filled citrate tube
Time between sampling and testing
The reagent's sensitivity, corrected by the INR calculation
inr.rangeNote: On warfarin the INR is read against the person's individual target range; off anticoagulants a value near 1.0 is expected, but the interpretation belongs to the clinician.

vitamin-b12.name: Vitamin B12
vitamin-b12.summary: The vitamin, absorbed with intrinsic factor in the last part of the small intestine, that the marrow needs to make red cells and nerves need to keep their myelin.
vitamin-b12.what: Vitamin B12 comes from animal foods and fortified products, is absorbed in the terminal ileum after binding to intrinsic factor made by the stomach, and is stored in the liver for years. Deficiency causes anaemia with large red cells and, independently, damage to peripheral nerves and the spinal cord.
higher: Supplements and injections
Liver disease
Some blood disorders
lower: Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor)
Vegan diets without supplementation
Stomach or ileal surgery, Crohn's disease, coeliac disease
Long-term metformin, proton-pump inhibitors or H2 blockers
Pregnancy and oral contraceptives (a measurement effect)
factors: Recent supplements mask deficiency
A wide borderline zone between clearly low and clearly normal
Assay interference in some people with intrinsic-factor antibodies
vitamin-b12.rangeNote: Read against the laboratory's interval; a borderline result is interpreted with symptoms, the blood count and sometimes further markers.

folate.name: Folate
folate.summary: The B vitamin from green vegetables and fortified foods that cells need to make DNA; deficiency causes anaemia with large red cells and, in early pregnancy, neural tube defects.
folate.what: Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine and stored only for a few months, so deficiency develops quickly when intake falls. Serum folate reflects recent intake; red cell folate reflects the previous few months. It works with vitamin B12, which is why the two are tested together and why B12 status must be known before folic acid is given.
higher: Supplements and fortified foods
Recent meals (serum folate)
lower: Poor diet and alcohol excess
Malabsorption: coeliac disease, Crohn's disease
Pregnancy and increased cell turnover
Methotrexate, some antiepileptics, trimethoprim
factors: A recent meal raises serum folate
Haemolysis of the sample releases red cell folate
Vitamin B12 deficiency can trap folate in an unusable form
folate.rangeNote: Read against the laboratory's interval for the sample type (serum or red cell), which differ.

vitamin-d-25-oh.name: 25-hydroxyvitamin D
vitamin-d-25-oh.summary: The storage form of vitamin D that the liver makes, the best single measure of vitamin D status and the value the vitamin D test reports.
vitamin-d-25-oh.what: Vitamin D made in the skin by sunlight or taken in food is converted in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which circulates for weeks; the kidney then activates a small fraction to calcitriol, the hormone that raises calcium absorption from the gut. The 25-hydroxy form is measured because it reflects the body's supply.
higher: Excess supplements (rarely, causing high calcium)
lower: Little sun exposure, darker skin, covering clothing, winter at high latitude
Low intake and malabsorption
Obesity, older age, chronic kidney and liver disease
Some antiepileptics and other medicines
factors: Season and latitude
The assay method, which changes results between laboratories
Recent high-dose supplements
vitamin-d-25-oh.rangeNote: Read against deficiency and adequacy cut-offs that differ slightly between guidelines, reported by the laboratory; not a population reference interval.

hcg.name: hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)
hcg.summary: The hormone made from implantation onwards by the trophoblast, the tissue that becomes the placenta. It is what pregnancy tests detect, and two blood levels about 48 hours apart, read with an ultrasound scan, show how an early pregnancy is behaving. Outside pregnancy it is a tumour marker.
hcg.what: Human chorionic gonadotropin is a glycoprotein whose beta subunit is unique to it, which is why laboratory tests measure beta-hCG. It is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the implanting embryo and later by the placenta, and keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone so that the endometrium is not shed, until the placenta takes over at about 10 to 12 weeks. hCG appears in blood within a few days of implantation and in urine at about the time of the missed period, when a home test becomes reliable. In a normally developing early pregnancy the level roughly doubles every two to three days, so what matters is the trend between two samples rather than any single value, read alongside an ultrasound scan and the person's symptoms. Sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or collapse in early pregnancy needs emergency assessment and should not wait for a repeat blood test.
hcg.unit: IU/L in the UK (international units per litre), reported as mIU/mL in the United States, where 1 mIU/mL is the same as 1 IU/L; urine tests are reported as positive or negative rather than as a number
higher: Pregnancy: the level rises steeply with gestational age in the first weeks and is the basis of every pregnancy test
A multiple pregnancy, in which the level is higher than expected for the dates
A molar pregnancy and other gestational trophoblastic disease, in which the level is often very high and fails to fall as expected
Germ cell tumours of the testis or ovary, and rarely other cancers, where hCG serves as a tumour marker
A recent pregnancy, miscarriage or termination, after which the level takes days to weeks to fall, so a test can stay positive for a time
Fertility treatment using an injection that contains hCG to trigger ovulation
lower: An ectopic pregnancy, in which the level often rises more slowly than expected or plateaus instead of doubling; a normal rise does not rule an ectopic pregnancy out, and hCG cannot show where a pregnancy is, so pain or bleeding in early pregnancy needs assessment in an early pregnancy unit whatever the number does
Miscarriage, in which the level falls
A pregnancy earlier than the dates suggest, or a test done too soon after conception, when the level is still below what the test can detect
The second and third trimesters of a normal pregnancy, when the level falls from its first-trimester peak to a lower plateau
A falling level after treatment of a molar pregnancy or a germ cell tumour, which is the sign that treatment is working
factors: How long it is since implantation: a urine test taken before the missed period can be negative in a perfectly normal pregnancy and should be repeated
Dilute urine, which is why the first urine of the day is advised when testing early
Fertility treatment containing hCG, which can keep a test positive for several days after the injection
Rare interfering antibodies in blood, which can give a persistently positive result with no pregnancy or tumour to explain it
The assay and the units differ between laboratories, so a series of results should be compared only within the same laboratory
hcg.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

oestradiol.name: Oestradiol
oestradiol.summary: The main oestrogen of the reproductive years, made chiefly by the growing ovarian follicle and, in smaller amounts, by the testes and by aromatase in fat and other tissues acting on adrenal and gonadal androgens. It is read with the day of the cycle and with LH and FSH, and is used to monitor oestrogen treatment, including gender-affirming feminising therapy.
oestradiol.what: Oestradiol is the most active of the oestrogens. In women it is made chiefly by the granulosa cells of the developing ovarian follicle, which use aromatase to convert androgens supplied by the neighbouring theca cells; the steep rise late in the follicular phase triggers the luteinising hormone (LH) surge and ovulation, and after ovulation the corpus luteum makes oestradiol alongside progesterone. The level swings several-fold across a normal cycle, so a result means little without the day of the cycle beside it and is usually read with LH and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). People assigned male at birth make oestradiol too: a little from the testes and most from aromatase in fat, muscle, bone and brain acting on testosterone. Only the fraction not bound to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin acts on tissues.
oestradiol.unit: pmol/L in the UK, pg/mL in the United States (1 pg/mL is about 3.7 pmol/L)
higher: The late follicular phase and the luteal phase of a normal cycle: oestradiol peaks just before ovulation and rises again after it
Pregnancy, in which the placenta becomes the main source
Oestrogen treatment: hormone replacement therapy, feminising gender-affirming therapy, and the ovarian stimulation used in fertility treatment
Oestrogen-producing tumours of the ovary or adrenal gland, suspected when a high level cannot be explained by the cycle, pregnancy or treatment
Obesity, in which aromatase in fat converts more androgen to oestradiol, and liver disease, which slows clearance and raises the binding protein
In men, a raised level forms part of the investigation of gynaecomastia
lower: The menopause and the years after it, when the follicles are exhausted: oestradiol falls while FSH climbs
Premature ovarian insufficiency, the same picture arising before the age of 40
Hypothalamic amenorrhoea from low body weight, heavy training, stress or serious illness, in which LH and FSH are low as well
Disease of the pituitary or hypothalamus, and Turner syndrome, in which the ovaries do not develop normally
Medicines that block or suppress oestrogen production, such as aromatase inhibitors and GnRH analogues
Masculinising hormone therapy in trans men and non-binary people taking testosterone
factors: The day of the cycle: the result cannot be interpreted without it, which is why the request form asks for the date of the last period

The menopause in women over 45 is diagnosed from symptoms and the pattern of periods, not from a blood test; when periods stop before 40, or between 40 and 45 with menopausal symptoms, NICE recommends FSH testing, and oestradiol is interpreted alongside it rather than on its own
Pregnancy and breastfeeding
Combined hormonal contraception, which suppresses the ovary's own production; the synthetic ethinylestradiol it contains is not measured by the assay
Time of day, and in people on treatment the interval since the last patch change, gel application, tablet or injection
The assay: immunoassays are imprecise at the low levels found in men, children and after the menopause, where mass spectrometry is preferred
oestradiol.rangeNote: Reference intervals for this marker depend on the laboratory, the assay, the units, age, sex and pregnancy. Interpret a result against the interval printed on the laboratory report, not against a figure from the internet.

testosterone.name: Testosterone
testosterone.summary: The principal androgen, made mainly by the testes and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands. Its blood level is measured to investigate suspected hypogonadism in men and hyperandrogenism in women, and to guide and monitor testosterone treatment and gender-affirming hormone therapy.
testosterone.what: In the testes, Leydig cells make testosterone under the control of luteinising hormone (LH) from the pituitary, which is itself driven by pulses of GnRH from the hypothalamus; testosterone, and the oestradiol made from it, feed back to restrain LH and FSH. In women the hormone comes from the ovaries, the adrenal glands and the conversion of adrenal precursors in fat and skin, at a small fraction of the male level. Most testosterone in blood is tightly bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG); the rest is loosely bound to albumin or free, and it is this free and albumin-bound (bioavailable) fraction that reaches tissues, so laboratories report total testosterone and add a free, calculated free or bioavailable value when SHBG is likely to be abnormal. Some target tissues convert it to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT) by 5-alpha-reductase, and fat and other tissues convert some to oestradiol by aromatase. The level is highest in the early morning and falls through the day, so a morning sample is standard, and a low result is repeated before hypogonadism is diagnosed. In gender-affirming care the level shows whether treatment has brought testosterone into the reference range of the affirmed gender, and in a person on testosterone it is read together with the haematocrit.
testosterone.unit: nmol/L in the UK, ng/dL in the United States (1 nmol/L is about 29 ng/dL)
higher: Polycystic ovary syndrome, the commonest cause of a mildly raised level in women
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumours of the ovary or adrenal gland, suspected when the rise is marked or rapid and comes with virilisation
Testosterone treatment and misuse of testosterone preparations (other anabolic steroids suppress the body's own testosterone and can give a low result)
Masculinising hormone therapy in trans men and non-binary people, where the aim is a level within the male reference range

Raised sex hormone-binding globulin, as in hyperthyroidism, pregnancy or oestrogen replacement therapy, which raises the total level while the free fraction is unchanged or lower (combined hormonal contraception raises SHBG but lowers both total and free testosterone)
lower: Primary hypogonadism: failure of the testes themselves from Klinefelter syndrome, undescended testes, mumps orchitis, chemotherapy, radiotherapy or injury, with high LH and FSH
Secondary hypogonadism: disease of the pituitary or hypothalamus, including tumours, high prolactin and iron overload, with LH and FSH low or inappropriately normal
Ageing, obesity, type 2 diabetes, long-term illness and obstructive sleep apnoea
Opioids, glucocorticoids, GnRH analogues and anti-androgens such as cyproterone acetate (receptor-blocking anti-androgens such as bicalutamide can instead raise the measured level)

Removal of the testes (orchidectomy), including as part of vaginoplasty, after which anti-androgen treatment is usually stopped by the specialist team; and removal of the ovaries in people not taking testosterone
Feminising hormone therapy in trans women and non-binary people, where oestradiol with an anti-androgen or GnRH analogue is used to bring the level into the female reference range
factors: Time of day: the level peaks in the early morning and falls through the day, so a fasting morning sample is standard and a low result is repeated before hypogonadism is diagnosed

SHBG: total testosterone rises and falls with the binding protein, which is raised by oestrogen, thyroid excess, ageing and liver disease and lowered by obesity and insulin resistance, so a free or calculated free value may be needed
Acute illness, short sleep and a recent meal can lower the level temporarily
Assay: immunoassays are less accurate at the low levels found in women, children and trans women on treatment, where mass spectrometry is preferred
In people on treatment, the timing of the sample relative to the last injection or gel application

meta.name: Drug targets
meta.about: Biological targets: the receptors, enzymes, ion channels, transporters and pathways that medicines act on. Each page explains what the target does in the body, where it is found, which medicines and drug classes act on it and which physiology and conditions it connects to. The bridge between a medicine and the anatomy it changes.

l-type-calcium-channel.name: L-type calcium channel
l-type-calcium-channel.summary: A voltage-gated channel in the membrane of smooth-muscle and heart-muscle cells that lets calcium in when the cell is electrically excited. Calcium entry is what makes the muscle contract, so blocking the channel relaxes artery walls and, for some drugs, slows the heart.
l-type-calcium-channel.what: L-type ('long-lasting') calcium channels open when the membrane depolarises and stay open long enough for a substantial calcium current. In vascular smooth muscle the calcium that enters activates the contractile proteins directly, setting the tone of arterioles and therefore blood pressure. In heart muscle the same channel triggers a much larger release of calcium from internal stores with each beat, and in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes it carries the current that generates and conducts the heartbeat. The dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine) bind a site on the channel that is favoured in relaxed, depolarised vascular muscle, so they dilate arteries with little effect on the heart; verapamil and diltiazem bind differently and also slow the heart's nodes.
l-type-calcium-channel.role: Sets arteriolar tone (blood pressure), drives cardiac contraction and conduction through the AV node, and contributes to insulin release and neurotransmitter release elsewhere in the body.
l-type-calcium-channel.location: Cell membranes of vascular smooth muscle in arterioles and arteries, cardiac muscle and the heart's conduction tissue; also endocrine and nerve cells.

at1-receptor.name: Angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor
at1-receptor.summary: The receptor through which angiotensin II constricts arteries, releases aldosterone and drives the thickening of heart and vessel walls. Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, candesartan, valsartan) occupy it so that angiotensin II cannot act.
at1-receptor.what: Angiotensin II is the final product of the renin–angiotensin system, released whenever the kidney senses low pressure or low salt. Acting on AT1 receptors it narrows arterioles within seconds, prompts the adrenal cortex to secrete aldosterone (which makes the kidney retain salt and water), constricts the efferent arteriole of the glomerulus to hold up filtration pressure, stimulates thirst and sympathetic activity, and over months promotes growth and fibrosis in the heart, arteries and kidney. Blocking AT1 therefore lowers blood pressure, reduces the strain on a failing heart, lowers pressure inside the glomerulus (which protects diabetic kidneys but can drop filtration if the renal arteries are narrowed) and raises potassium by removing the aldosterone signal. ACE inhibitors act one step upstream by preventing angiotensin II from being made at all.
at1-receptor.role: Vasoconstriction, aldosterone release, sodium and water retention, glomerular pressure control and long-term cardiovascular remodelling.
at1-receptor.location: Vascular smooth muscle, the adrenal cortex (zona glomerulosa), the kidney's afferent and efferent arterioles and tubules, the heart, the brain and the sympathetic nerve endings.

angiotensin-converting-enzyme.name: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.summary: The enzyme on the surface of blood-vessel lining cells, above all in the lungs, that converts inactive angiotensin I into angiotensin II and also breaks down bradykinin. ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, ramipril) block it, lowering blood pressure and protecting the heart and kidneys.
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.what: Renin from the kidney clips angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, which is inactive until ACE removes two amino acids to make angiotensin II. ACE sits on endothelial cells throughout the circulation, most densely in the pulmonary capillaries, so a single pass through the lungs activates the hormone. The same enzyme inactivates bradykinin, a peptide that widens vessels and, in the airways, irritates cough receptors. Inhibiting ACE therefore lowers angiotensin II (less constriction, less aldosterone, lower glomerular pressure) and raises bradykinin (extra vasodilation, but also the dry cough that affects around one in ten people and the rare but dangerous swelling of angioedema). Because angiotensin II can still be made by other enzymes, ARBs that block the receptor itself are the alternative when the cough is intolerable.
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.role: Activation of the renin–angiotensin system (angiotensin II production) and inactivation of bradykinin.
angiotensin-converting-enzyme.location: The luminal surface of endothelial cells lining blood vessels, particularly the pulmonary capillaries; also kidney tubules, gut, brain and testis.

hmg-coa-reductase.name: HMG-CoA reductase
hmg-coa-reductase.summary: The enzyme that controls the speed of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Statins block it, so liver cells make less cholesterol and pull more LDL out of the blood, lowering LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart attack and stroke.
hmg-coa-reductase.what: Cholesterol is built in a long chain of reactions, and the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate by HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting step and the point the cell regulates. Statins are close mimics of HMG-CoA that sit in the enzyme's active site. When synthesis falls, the liver cell senses low cholesterol and responds by displaying more LDL receptors on its surface, which capture LDL particles from the blood; that receptor response, more than the fall in synthesis itself, is what lowers LDL cholesterol by 30 to 55% depending on the statin and dose. The enzyme is present in every cell, but statins are taken up mostly by the liver, which is why their main effects and most of their side effects (including the rise in liver enzymes) relate to it. Muscle symptoms are thought to involve the same pathway in muscle cells.
hmg-coa-reductase.role: Rate-limiting step of cholesterol biosynthesis; its inhibition upregulates hepatic LDL receptors.
hmg-coa-reductase.location: The endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells (hepatocytes), and at lower levels in all nucleated cells.

cox-1.name: Cyclo-oxygenase 1 (COX-1)
cox-1.summary: The 'housekeeping' form of cyclo-oxygenase, present all the time in platelets, the stomach lining and the kidney. It makes the thromboxane that lets platelets clump and the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and keep the kidneys perfused; aspirin and other NSAIDs block it.
cox-1.what: Cyclo-oxygenases convert arachidonic acid released from cell membranes into the prostaglandins and thromboxane that act as short-range messengers. COX-1 is constitutive: it is always present and supplies the everyday prostaglandins that keep the stomach lining coated in mucus and bicarbonate, maintain blood flow through the kidney when the body is stressed, and, in platelets, make thromboxane A2, the signal that recruits other platelets to a clot. Low-dose aspirin acetylates COX-1 irreversibly; because platelets have no nucleus they cannot replace the enzyme, so a small daily dose suppresses thromboxane for the platelet's whole life. Non-selective NSAIDs such as ibuprofen block COX-1 reversibly, which explains their shared risks: stomach ulcers and bleeding, reduced kidney perfusion in the dehydrated, and a temporary antiplatelet effect that can interfere with aspirin's.
cox-1.role: Platelet aggregation (thromboxane A2), gastric mucosal protection and renal blood flow (prostaglandins).
cox-1.location: Platelets, the gastric and duodenal mucosa, the kidney and vascular endothelium; present in most tissues at a basal level.

cox-2.name: Cyclo-oxygenase 2 (COX-2)
cox-2.summary: The inducible form of cyclo-oxygenase, switched on at sites of injury and inflammation and in the brain during fever. Its prostaglandins sensitise pain nerves, widen inflamed vessels and reset the body's thermostat; NSAIDs relieve pain, swelling and fever by blocking it.
cox-2.what: COX-2 is barely present in most resting tissues but is induced within hours by cytokines and growth factors wherever tissue is damaged or inflamed, and in the hypothalamus in response to the pyrogens of infection. Its prostaglandins (mainly PGE2 and prostacyclin) lower the threshold of pain fibres, dilate vessels and increase their leakiness (redness, warmth, swelling), and raise the hypothalamic set-point that produces fever. Ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac block COX-2 and COX-1 together; celecoxib and etoricoxib block COX-2 selectively and spare the stomach, but because COX-2 also makes the prostacyclin that keeps the vessel lining anti-thrombotic (unlike platelet thromboxane, which is COX-1), selective inhibition tilts the balance towards clotting, the basis of the cardiovascular warnings on all NSAIDs. COX-2 is also constitutive in the kidney and in healing tissue, which is why NSAIDs can impair kidney function and delay ulcer healing.
cox-2.role: Inflammatory prostaglandin production: pain sensitisation, vasodilation and oedema in inflamed tissue, fever; vascular prostacyclin and renal prostaglandins.
cox-2.location: Induced in inflamed and injured tissue (joints, skin, gut, muscle), macrophages and the hypothalamus; constitutively present in the kidney, vascular endothelium and brain.

serotonin-transporter.name: Serotonin transporter (SERT)
serotonin-transporter.summary: The pump on the presynaptic nerve ending that clears serotonin from the synapse after it has been released. SSRIs such as sertraline block it, so serotonin stays in the synapse longer; the antidepressant effect follows over weeks as receptors and circuits adapt.
serotonin-transporter.what: Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) released into a synapse acts on receptors on the next neuron and is then recycled by the serotonin transporter, a membrane protein that carries it back into the releasing nerve ending. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors bind the transporter and stop that recycling within hours of the first dose, yet mood improvement takes two to six weeks, which shows that the benefit comes from slower downstream changes in receptor sensitivity, gene expression and neural plasticity rather than from the raised serotonin itself. The same transporter is present on platelets, where blocking it depletes their serotonin and slightly impairs clotting (a reason bleeding risk rises when SSRIs are combined with NSAIDs or anticoagulants), and in the gut wall, where serotonin regulates motility (nausea and bowel changes early in treatment). Combining several serotonergic drugs can over-stimulate serotonin receptors and cause serotonin syndrome.
serotonin-transporter.role: Terminates serotonin signalling by reuptake into presynaptic neurons; also loads serotonin into platelets.
serotonin-transporter.location: Presynaptic membranes of serotonergic neurons originating in the brainstem raphe nuclei and projecting throughout the brain; platelet membranes; enterochromaffin cells and nerves of the gut wall.

beta-1-adrenoceptor.name: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor
beta-1-adrenoceptor.summary: The receptor in heart muscle and the heart's pacemaker tissue through which adrenaline and noradrenaline speed the heart and strengthen its contraction. Beta blockers occupy it to slow the heart, lower its oxygen demand and protect it after a heart attack and in heart failure.
beta-1-adrenoceptor.what: Sympathetic nerves and the adrenal medulla act on the heart through beta-1 receptors on the sinoatrial node (faster rate), the atrioventricular node (faster conduction) and the muscle of the atria and ventricles (stronger contraction and faster relaxation). Beta-1 receptors on the kidney's juxtaglomerular cells also release renin. Blocking them reduces heart rate and contractility, which cuts the heart's oxygen consumption (the basis of angina relief), suppresses abnormal rhythms, lowers blood pressure partly through less renin, and in chronic heart failure protects the myocardium from sustained sympathetic overdrive. Cardioselective beta blockers such as bisoprolol and metoprolol prefer beta-1 over the beta-2 receptors of the airways, though selectivity is relative and asthma remains a caution. Sudden withdrawal after long use can rebound with tachycardia and angina because the receptors have become more numerous.
beta-1-adrenoceptor.role: Increases heart rate, conduction velocity and contractility in response to catecholamines; stimulates renin release.
beta-1-adrenoceptor.location: Sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, atrial and ventricular myocardium, and the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney.

beta-2-adrenoceptor.name: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor
beta-2-adrenoceptor.summary: The receptor on airway smooth muscle through which adrenaline relaxes the bronchi. Salbutamol and other beta-2 agonists stimulate it to open the airways in asthma and COPD; non-selective beta blockers block it and can provoke bronchospasm.
beta-2-adrenoceptor.what: Beta-2 receptors respond mainly to circulating adrenaline rather than to direct nerve supply. In bronchial smooth muscle they raise cyclic AMP, which relaxes the muscle and widens the airway within minutes; they also increase mucociliary clearance and stabilise mast cells. In skeletal muscle they cause tremor and drive potassium into cells (high-dose salbutamol lowers blood potassium), in the liver they release glucose, in the uterus they relax the muscle, and in blood vessels supplying muscle they dilate. Short-acting agonists such as salbutamol act for about four hours as relievers; long-acting agonists (salmeterol, formoterol) last twelve hours or more and are combined with inhaled corticosteroids, because used alone in asthma they can mask worsening inflammation. Frequent use down-regulates the receptors, one reason reliever overuse signals poorly controlled asthma.
beta-2-adrenoceptor.role: Bronchodilation, vasodilation in skeletal muscle, glycogen breakdown, uterine relaxation and potassium uptake into cells.
beta-2-adrenoceptor.location: Smooth muscle of the bronchi and bronchioles, vascular smooth muscle in skeletal muscle beds, the uterus, liver and skeletal muscle cells, and mast cells.

proton-pump.name: Gastric proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase)
proton-pump.summary: The enzyme in the stomach's parietal cells that pumps acid into the stomach as the final step of acid secretion. Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole disable it, cutting acid output by more than 90% and allowing ulcers and reflux oesophagitis to heal.
proton-pump.what: Parietal cells in the glands of the stomach body secrete hydrochloric acid by swapping potassium for hydrogen ions across their apical membrane using the H+/K+ ATPase, an energy-consuming pump that can create a million-fold concentration gradient. Histamine, gastrin and the vagus nerve each stimulate the cell through separate receptors, but all three converge on this pump, which is why blocking it suppresses acid more completely than blocking any one signal (H2 blockers such as famotidine block only the histamine route). Proton pump inhibitors are inactive prodrugs that concentrate in the acid canaliculus of the parietal cell, are converted there and bind the pump irreversibly; acid secretion only returns once new pumps are synthesised, so a once-daily dose taken before breakfast works around the clock. Long-term loss of acid raises gastrin, changes the gut flora and modestly reduces absorption of magnesium, vitamin B12, iron and calcium.
proton-pump.role: Final common step of gastric acid secretion.
proton-pump.location: The apical (canalicular) membrane of parietal cells in the oxyntic glands of the stomach body and fundus.

penicillin-binding-proteins.name: Penicillin-binding proteins
penicillin-binding-proteins.summary: Bacterial enzymes that cross-link the peptidoglycan mesh of the cell wall as bacteria grow. Penicillins, cephalosporins and other beta-lactam antibiotics bind them, the wall weakens and the bacterium bursts; human cells have no cell wall, so the drugs spare them.
penicillin-binding-proteins.what: The bacterial cell wall is a single giant molecule of peptidoglycan, sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides, that holds the cell together against its own high internal pressure. Penicillin-binding proteins are the transpeptidases that make those cross-links, and beta-lactam antibiotics mimic the natural substrate closely enough to bind the active site permanently. Growing bacteria with unfinished walls then lyse, which is why beta-lactams work best on actively dividing organisms and why they are bactericidal. Resistance arises when bacteria make beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug (countered by clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav), alter their PBPs so the drug no longer binds (the mechanism of MRSA and penicillin-resistant pneumococci), or, in Gram-negative organisms, restrict entry through their outer membrane. Because the target does not exist in humans, side effects come from allergy and from disruption of the body's own bacterial flora rather than from the mechanism itself.
penicillin-binding-proteins.role: Synthesis and remodelling of bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan (transpeptidation).
penicillin-binding-proteins.location: The cytoplasmic membrane of bacteria, facing the cell wall; absent from human cells.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

bacterial-ribosome.name: Bacterial ribosome (50S subunit)
bacterial-ribosome.summary: The protein-making machinery of bacteria, built differently enough from the human ribosome to be a selective drug target. Macrolides such as azithromycin bind the 50S subunit and stop the bacterium making proteins, halting its growth.
bacterial-ribosome.what: Every cell makes protein on ribosomes, but bacterial ribosomes (70S, made of 30S and 50S subunits) differ from human cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S) in their RNA and proteins, so antibiotics can bind them selectively. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) bind the 23S ribosomal RNA in the exit tunnel of the 50S subunit and block the growing peptide chain from leaving, which stops protein synthesis; the effect is mainly bacteriostatic, leaving the immune system to clear the organism. Because macrolides reach very high concentrations inside cells, they are effective against intracellular organisms such as Chlamydia, Mycoplasma and Legionella that penicillins cannot reach. Other classes target the ribosome at different sites: tetracyclines and aminoglycosides on the 30S subunit, clindamycin and linezolid on the 50S. Human mitochondria have ribosomes of bacterial ancestry, which may contribute to some antibiotic toxicities. Resistance follows methylation of the binding site or efflux pumps.
bacterial-ribosome.role: Bacterial protein synthesis (translation); inhibition halts bacterial growth.
bacterial-ribosome.location: The cytoplasm of bacteria; not present in human cytoplasm (mitochondrial ribosomes are related but distinct).

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

hepatic-glucose-production.name: Hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis)
hepatic-glucose-production.summary: The liver's manufacture and release of glucose between meals, from lactate, amino acids and glycerol. In type 2 diabetes this output runs too high; metformin's main action is to reduce it, which lowers fasting blood glucose without causing hypoglycaemia.
hepatic-glucose-production.what: Between meals and overnight the liver keeps blood glucose steady, first by releasing stored glycogen and then by making new glucose (gluconeogenesis) from lactate, alanine and glycerol. Insulin normally restrains this; in type 2 diabetes the liver is insulin-resistant and keeps producing glucose even when levels are already high, which is the main reason fasting glucose rises. Metformin accumulates in hepatocytes and lowers their energy state (through effects on mitochondrial respiration and the energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase, and on the redox balance that gluconeogenesis depends on), which switches gluconeogenesis down and modestly increases insulin sensitivity in muscle. Because it does not push the pancreas to release insulin, metformin does not cause low blood sugar on its own. The same reliance on mitochondrial function underlies its rare serious harm: when the drug accumulates in kidney failure or severe illness, lactate that the liver would normally convert to glucose builds up (lactic acidosis).
hepatic-glucose-production.role: Maintains blood glucose during fasting; excessive output drives fasting hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes.
hepatic-glucose-production.location: Hepatocytes, particularly those around the portal tracts; the kidney cortex contributes a smaller share.

mu-opioid-receptor.name: Mu-opioid receptor
mu-opioid-receptor.summary: The receptor through which morphine and the other opioids relieve pain, and also the one responsible for their sedation, slowed breathing, constipation, euphoria and dependence. The body's own endorphins act on the same receptor.
mu-opioid-receptor.what: Mu-opioid receptors sit on nerve cells in the spinal cord's dorsal horn, in the brainstem and midbrain, in the limbic system and in the gut wall. Activation reduces the release of pain transmitters in the spinal cord, switches on descending pathways from the brainstem that dampen pain signals, and changes how the pain is experienced in the brain, so the pain is still detected but matters less. The same receptors in the medulla blunt the response to rising carbon dioxide, which is why overdose kills by stopping breathing and why naloxone, which displaces opioids from the receptor, reverses it within minutes. In the gut they slow motility and tighten sphincters, causing the constipation that does not fade with time. Repeated stimulation leads to tolerance (more drug for the same effect) and physical dependence, with withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped abruptly. Codeine and tramadol are weaker or partial agonists; buprenorphine is a partial agonist used in dependence treatment.
mu-opioid-receptor.role: Analgesia, sedation, respiratory depression, reduced gut motility, euphoria and reward; tolerance and dependence with sustained use.
mu-opioid-receptor.location: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord, periaqueductal grey and medulla of the brainstem, thalamus, limbic system and the enteric nerves of the gut wall.

h1-receptor.name: Histamine H1 receptor
h1-receptor.summary: The receptor through which histamine, released from mast cells in an allergic reaction, causes itching, sneezing, a runny nose, swelling and hives. Antihistamines such as cetirizine block it; older antihistamines also reach H1 receptors in the brain and cause drowsiness.
h1-receptor.what: When an allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells in the skin, nose, airways or gut, the cells release histamine within minutes. Acting on H1 receptors, histamine widens small vessels and makes them leak (redness and swelling, the wheal of a hive), stimulates itch and pain nerve endings, contracts bronchial and gut smooth muscle and increases mucus secretion. H1 antagonists compete for the receptor (technically as inverse agonists) and relieve the itch, sneezing and rhinorrhoea of hay fever and urticaria, but they do little for the airway narrowing of asthma, which involves many other mediators. First-generation antihistamines (chlorphenamine, promethazine) cross the blood–brain barrier, where H1 receptors help maintain wakefulness, so they sedate and impair driving; second-generation drugs (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) are kept out of the brain by transporters and cause far less drowsiness. Histamine's other receptors do different jobs: H2 drives stomach acid, H3 and H4 modulate nerves and immune cells.
h1-receptor.role: Mediates the acute allergic response (vasodilation, vascular leak, itch, bronchoconstriction, mucus) and contributes to wakefulness in the brain.
h1-receptor.location: Endothelium and smooth muscle of small blood vessels, sensory nerve endings in the skin and mucosa, bronchial and gut smooth muscle, and neurons in the brain.

vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.name: Vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1)
vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.summary: The liver enzyme that recycles vitamin K so it can activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Warfarin blocks it, so the liver releases inactive clotting factors and blood clots more slowly; the effect builds over days and is measured with the INR.
vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.what: Four clotting factors and two anticoagulant proteins (C and S) are only functional after a vitamin K-dependent step that adds carboxyl groups to them; each cycle oxidises vitamin K, and VKORC1 reduces it back for reuse. Warfarin inhibits VKORC1, vitamin K becomes unavailable, and newly made factors are released as inactive precursors. Because circulating factors are only replaced as they decay (factor VII within hours, prothrombin over two to three days), anticoagulation takes several days to develop and heparin cover is used at the start; the temporary early fall of protein C can even make clotting worse briefly. The dose needed varies many-fold between people, partly because of common variants in the VKORC1 and CYP2C9 genes, and it is disturbed by dietary vitamin K (green vegetables), alcohol, illness and a very long list of interacting drugs, hence the need for regular INR monitoring. Vitamin K itself, given by mouth or injection, reverses warfarin over hours; clotting factor concentrates do so immediately.
vitamin-k-epoxide-reductase.role: Regeneration of reduced vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.

factor-xa.name: Factor Xa
factor-xa.summary: The clotting enzyme at the junction of the two arms of the coagulation cascade, which converts prothrombin into thrombin. Apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban block it directly, preventing clots in atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism without the monitoring warfarin needs.
factor-xa.what: Coagulation proceeds as a chain of enzyme activations that all converge on factor X. Once activated to factor Xa, it assembles with factor Va on the surface of platelets to form the prothrombinase complex, which generates thrombin, and thrombin then converts fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh of a clot and amplifies its own production. Each molecule of Xa yields many molecules of thrombin, so blocking Xa is an efficient way to reduce clotting. Direct oral anticoagulants bind the active site of Xa reversibly, take effect within hours, and have predictable dosing that does not require INR checks, although kidney function, body weight and interacting drugs (strong inhibitors or inducers of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein) affect their levels. Low-molecular-weight heparins such as enoxaparin inhibit Xa indirectly through antithrombin. Andexanet alfa is a specific reversal agent; bleeding is the shared main risk of every drug in this pathway, and it multiplies when they are combined with antiplatelets or NSAIDs.
factor-xa.role: Conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, the amplifying step of the coagulation cascade.
factor-xa.location: Circulating in plasma as inactive factor X; activated on the surface of platelets and damaged endothelium at the site of injury.

nkcc2.name: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2)
nkcc2.summary: The transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle that reabsorbs sodium, potassium and chloride from the filtrate. Loop diuretics such as furosemide block it, so the kidney passes far more salt and water, relieving the fluid overload of heart failure.
nkcc2.what: About a quarter of the sodium the kidney filters is reclaimed in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle by NKCC2, which carries one sodium, one potassium and two chloride ions together from the tubular fluid into the cell. Because this segment is impermeable to water, the salt it removes also builds the concentration gradient in the kidney medulla that later allows urine to be concentrated. Loop diuretics reach the transporter from the tubular side (they are secreted into the tubule by the proximal cells, so they still work when filtration is poor) and block it; salt that stays in the tubule drags water with it, the medullary gradient collapses, and a large, dilute diuresis follows within an hour of a dose. The lost potassium, magnesium and calcium explain the electrolyte disturbances of loop diuretics, the fall in blood volume explains dizziness and rising creatinine, and the same transporter in the inner ear accounts for their rare ototoxicity at high doses. NSAIDs blunt the effect by reducing the prostaglandins that support it.
nkcc2.role: Reabsorbs about 25% of filtered sodium and chloride and generates the medullary concentration gradient; also reabsorbs potassium, calcium and magnesium indirectly.
nkcc2.location: Apical membrane of the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle in the kidney; a related isoform is in the inner ear.
